Autonomic Cloud Resilience Through Brownout-Based Graceful Degradation: A Simulation-Based Evaluation of Brownout-Aware Load Balancing
Hari Prasad L, Yeruva Mahesh Reddy, and K. Ram Charan
Department of Computer Science and Engineering and Department of Data Science and AI Engineering, Indian Institute of Information Technology Dharwad, Karnataka 580009, India
Email: {23bds022, 23bcs136, 23bds029}@iiitdwd.ac.in
Preprint Working Paper • Target: IEEE Transactions on Cloud Computing / ACM TAAS • Date: November 2026

Abstract—Modern cloud-native architectures face persistent resilience challenges arising from sudden traffic surges (flash crowds) and abrupt compute instance crashes. Traditional mitigation relies heavily on physical hardware over-provisioning—which is economically and computationally resource-intensive—or reactive auto-scaling, which exhibits non-negligible provisioning delays that leave services vulnerable to queue saturation, tail latency inflation, and cascading timeouts during the onset of a shock [1, 5]. Autonomic brownout-based graceful degradation addresses these limitations by dynamically modulating the execution of optional software features (e.g., recommendation engines, real-time analytics) via a dynamic control variable known as the dimmer (θ∈[0,1]\theta \in [0, 1]θ∈[0,1]), thereby bounding service response times within strict Service Level Agreements (SLAs). However, when brownout controllers operate independently on distributed worker nodes under conventional load balancing policies like Join-Shortest-Queue (JSQ), an acute routing pathology emerges: degraded workers process requests rapidly by shedding optional tasks, emptying their queues quickly and drawing disproportionately high request volumes, which induces severe cluster load skew and delays post-failure recovery.

In this paper, we propose and evaluate CloudRescue, an autonomic cloud resilience architecture designed and evaluated via a high-fidelity discrete-event simulation model. CloudRescue integrates a discrete velocity-form Proportional-Integral (PI) feedback controller with intrinsic anti-windup output clamping on each worker node with Brownout-Aware Load Balancing (BALB) at the ingress proxy. BALB incorporates a composite multi-attribute dispatch scoring function that balances worker dimmer elasticity (θ\thetaθ), normalized queue backlog (q/Qmax⁡q / Q_{\max}q/Qmax​), and historical processor utilization (UUU), augmented with anti-overloading penalties and a soft-overload fallback mechanism. To rigorously isolate the individual and combined effects of local brownout adaptation and brownout-aware routing, we execute a comprehensive three-way ablation experiment across four stress scenarios (Nominal, Flash Crowd, Server Failure, and Compound Stress) spanning 360 primary simulation runs (30 independent pseudo-random seeds per condition) with deterministic Common Random Numbers (CRN) stream isolation.

Our empirical evaluation demonstrates that brownout adaptation decisively protects cloud service availability and response latency, reducing overall SLA failures by up to 41.10 percentage points (from 44.04%44.04%44.04% to 2.94%2.94%2.94%, p<10−60p < 10^{-60}p<10−60) under flash crowd stress and accelerating post-restoration recovery by 2.06×2.06\times2.06× to 2.15×2.15\times2.15× (p<4.1×10−5p < 4.1 \times 10^{-5}p<4.1×10−5) under empirical nominal-referenced recovery criteria (DEC-010). Crucially, our findings characterize a fundamental architectural trade-off between workload distribution equity and service fidelity: while BALB substantially mitigates the JSQ routing skew by restoring near-perfect load balance across active workers (J≥0.985J \ge 0.985J≥0.985 vs. J≈0.610–0.764J \approx 0.610\text{--}0.764J≈0.610–0.764, p<10−8p < 10^{-8}p<10−8), it does so by intentionally driving a broader proportion of the cluster into degraded operation, reducing optional service fidelity by 11.411.411.4 to 15.915.915.9 percentage points (p<10−38p < 10^{-38}p<10−38). We present the formal architecture, algorithmic formulations, and reproducible discrete-event simulation framework, establishing actionable design principles for building resilient, SLA-compliant cloud microservices under extreme operating constraints.

Index Terms—Cloud Resilience, Autonomic Computing, Graceful Degradation, Brownout, Load Balancing, Feedback Control Theory, Discrete-Event Simulation, Tail Latency, Service Level Agreements.

I. INTRODUCTION

Cloud computing infrastructures have become the standard execution environment for mission-critical digital services, ranging from financial transaction processing and enterprise enterprise resource planning to e-commerce and media streaming. These distributed systems are governed by strict Service Level Agreements (SLAs) that contractually obligate service providers to deliver low response times and high availability, frequently defined as percentiles of latency (e.g., 95th-percentile response latency P95≤100 msP_{95} \le 100\text{ ms}P95​≤100 ms) alongside bounded client timeout rates. However, modern cloud applications operate under highly unpredictable, stochastic operating environments where operational conditions can deviate drastically from stationary nominal forecasts.

As synthesized in the comprehensive resilience survey by Welsh and Benkhelifa [1], cloud services are subjected to a continuous spectrum of operational challenges across physical, virtualized, and application domains. These challenges can be broadly categorized into two major phenomena:

  1. Demand-Side Shocks (Flash Crowds and Traffic Spikes): Unanticipated surges in inbound request arrival rates triggered by external events (e.g., breaking news, flash sales, coordinated client reconnections) that rapidly exceed the provisioned serving capacity of compute clusters.
  2. Capacity-Side Shocks (Server Dropouts and Infrastructure Outages): Abrupt hardware crashes, network interface failures, memory exhaustion events, or hypervisor evictions that suddenly take multiple worker nodes offline, halving or severely diminishing aggregate compute capacity while client request volumes remain elevated.

When these stress phenomena coincide—a situation denoted in this work as compound stress—unmanaged cloud systems experience catastrophic queuing degradation. Because queuing delay in multi-server systems scales non-linearly with traffic intensity as utilization approaches unity, request buffers rapidly saturate, leading to widespread head-of-line (HOL) blocking, connection timeouts, queue-full dropouts, and widespread SLA violations.

To maintain resilience, cloud providers have historically relied on two primary architectural strategies: static hardware over-provisioning and reactive horizontal auto-scaling. As Welsh and Benkhelifa [1] observe, static over-provisioning—maintaining pools of redundant, hot-standby instances to absorb peak loads—is economically inefficient and resource-intensive. Conversely, reactive auto-scaling mechanisms attempt to dynamically provision additional instances when monitored load metrics (e.g., CPU utilization) breach predefined thresholds. However, dynamic provisioning is inherently reactive and subject to non-negligible provisioning delays (such as virtual machine scheduling, OS booting, and runtime initialization) [1, 5]. During this transient provisioning gap, the unmitigated incoming workload can overwhelm active instances, leading to queue saturation, tail latency inflation, and cascading timeouts before new capacity is ready.

Recognizing these limitations, the autonomic computing community has explored graceful degradation paradigms, inspired by the electrical power grid's historical use of "brownouts"—temporary reductions in system voltage to prevent catastrophic, widespread blackouts during peak load events. Adapted to cloud software by Klein et al. [2, 3], the brownout programming paradigm decomposes application logic into two distinct components: a mandatory core that provides the essential business functionality (e.g., completing an e-commerce checkout, executing an account balance update) and one or more optional components that enhance user experience but are not strictly critical to task completion (e.g., personalized recommendation carousels, algorithmic search re-ranking, high-resolution media rendering). By adjusting a dynamic probability parameter termed the dimmer (θ∈[0,1]\theta \in [0, 1]θ∈[0,1]) via a closed-loop feedback controller, a brownout-compliant server dynamically sheds optional tasks during periods of congestion. This reduction in per-request computational burden shortens service times, instantly deflates queue backlogs, stabilizes latency below SLA limits, and prevents queue overflow, all without requiring external hardware provisioning.

While local brownout controllers effectively regulate individual server instances, deploying brownout across a multi-server cluster introduces a complex and counter-intuitive control interaction at the cluster load balancer. Conventional load balancing algorithms—most notably Join-Shortest-Queue (JSQ)—are agnostic to worker degradation states. When a worker node experiences high latency and its local brownout controller decrements its dimmer (θ→0\theta \to 0θ→0), that worker executes only mandatory code, dramatically reducing its service time. Consequently, its queue drains rapidly. JSQ observes this low queue depth and immediately routes a disproportionate surge of incoming traffic to the degraded worker. Meanwhile, healthier workers operating at full fidelity (θ=1.0\theta = 1.0θ=1.0) process requests more slowly, retain longer queues, and are starved of incoming requests. This produces severe cluster load skew, penalizes overall system throughput, and delays recovery after failures.

To resolve this conflict, Klein et al. [3] demonstrated that cluster load balancers must be made brownout-aware, coordinating dispatching decisions with local worker dimmer elasticity. However, their pioneering work evaluated specific heuristics within an empirical web-benchmark testbed (Rubis on lighttpd), leaving several foundational architectural questions open: How does brownout-aware routing perform under controlled, reproducible failure schedules? What are its exact multi-attribute scoring dynamics? And what are the rigorous statistical trade-offs between workload equity, service fidelity, and failure recovery speed?

In this research, we present CloudRescue, an autonomic cloud resilience architecture that unites local velocity-form discrete PI brownout controllers with a multi-attribute Brownout-Aware Load Balancing (BALB) algorithm. Evaluated within a deterministic, multi-stream discrete-event simulation model in Python (SimPy), CloudRescue addresses the limitations identified in the Welsh and Benkhelifa [1] survey. Through an extensive pre-registered experimental battery of 360 primary simulation runs, we perform a clean three-way ablation analysis isolating baseline operation (CFG-A), local brownout alone (CFG-B), and full brownout-aware load balancing (CFG-C).

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 3 details the problem statement, queuing model, and research objectives. Section 4 outlines the explicit research contributions of this work. Section 5 surveys related literature using the Welsh and Benkhelifa [1] taxonomy as a foundation. Section 6 presents the complete architectural specification of CloudRescue, including our multi-stream pseudo-random reproducibility framework, velocity-form PI controller, and BALB scoring formulations. Section 7 details the experimental methodology, factorial design, metric definitions, and statistical inference protocol. Subsequent sections present the empirical results, sensitivity analysis, and concluding discussion.

II. PROBLEM STATEMENT AND RESEARCH OBJECTIVES

A. Problem Formulation and Queuing Model

Consider a cloud microservice cluster consisting of MMM heterogeneous or homogeneous worker instances fronted by a centralized ingress load balancer (proxy). User requests arrive at the load balancer following a time-varying stochastic arrival process with instantaneous arrival rate λ(t)\lambda(t)λ(t). Each arriving request kkk is immediately dispatched to an operational worker instance w∈{0,1,…,M−1}w \in \{0, 1, \dots, M-1\}w∈{0,1,…,M−1}.

Each worker node www manages an independent finite first-in, first-out (FIFO) request queue with maximum buffer capacity Qmax⁡Q_{\max}Qmax​. The queue waiting time of request kkk on worker www is denoted by Wk,w=tstart,k−tarrive,kW_{k, w} = t_{\text{start}, k} - t_{\text{arrive}, k}Wk,w​=tstart,k​−tarrive,k​, where tarrive,kt_{\text{arrive}, k}tarrive,k​ is the arrival timestamp at the load balancer and tstart,kt_{\text{start}, k}tstart,k​ is the timestamp at which worker www initiates execution of request kkk. If an arriving request finds the target worker's queue full (qw(t)≥Qmax⁡q_w(t) \ge Q_{\max}qw​(t)≥Qmax​), the request is rejected immediately, recorded as a queue drop (Ndrop_queueN_{\text{drop\_queue}}Ndrop_queue​). Furthermore, client connections maintain a maximum allowable wait-time deadline TtimeoutT_{\text{timeout}}Ttimeout​ (200.0 ms200.0\text{ ms}200.0 ms). When request kkk reaches the head of the worker queue, if its elapsed waiting time exceeds the timeout threshold (Wk,w>TtimeoutW_{k, w} > T_{\text{timeout}}Wk,w​>Ttimeout​), the worker aborts the request without execution, recording a timeout drop (Ndrop_timeoutN_{\text{drop\_timeout}}Ndrop_timeout​).

Each admitted request kkk comprises two sequential processing components:

  1. Mandatory Base Service: Computationally necessary logic required for request correctness, characterized by execution duration Smand,k∼Exp(μmand)S_{\text{mand}, k} \sim \text{Exp}(\mu_{\text{mand}})Smand,k​∼Exp(μmand​).
  2. Optional Enhanced Service: Non-mandatory logic that enriches the service response, characterized by execution duration Sopt,k∼Exp(μopt)S_{\text{opt}, k} \sim \text{Exp}(\mu_{\text{opt}})Sopt,k​∼Exp(μopt​).

In an unmanaged baseline system, workers execute both mandatory and optional logic for all admitted requests, resulting in a total service duration Sk=Smand,k+Sopt,kS_k = S_{\text{mand}, k} + S_{\text{opt}, k}Sk​=Smand,k​+Sopt,k​ with expected service time:

E[Sk]=μmand−1+μopt−1\mathbb{E}[S_k] = \mu_{\text{mand}}^{-1} + \mu_{\text{opt}}^{-1}E[Sk​]=μmand−1​+μopt−1​
(1)

In our target microservice profile, μmand−1=10 ms\mu_{\text{mand}}^{-1} = 10\text{ ms}μmand−1​=10 ms and μopt−1=30 ms\mu_{\text{opt}}^{-1} = 30\text{ ms}μopt−1​=30 ms, yielding an expected execution duration of 40 ms40\text{ ms}40 ms per request under full fidelity. The total end-to-end response latency experienced by the client for a successfully completed request is:

Lk=Wk,w+SkL_k = W_{k, w} + S_kLk​=Wk,w​+Sk​
(2)

The contractual Service Level Agreement (SLA) stipulates that all successful responses must be delivered within a maximum latency threshold rSLA=100.0 msr_{\text{SLA}} = 100.0\text{ ms}rSLA​=100.0 ms. Any successful request with Lk>rSLAL_k > r_{\text{SLA}}Lk​>rSLA​ is classified as a latency SLA violation. Any request that is dropped due to buffer saturation, connection timeout, server crash, or latency violation constitutes an overall SLA failure.

B. System Instabilities Under Stress

Under nominal stationary conditions (λ=80 req/s\lambda = 80\text{ req/s}λ=80 req/s across M=4M=4M=4 instances), aggregate cluster service capacity is μtotal=4×(1/0.040 s)=100 req/s\mu_{\text{total}} = 4 \times (1 / 0.040\text{ s}) = 100\text{ req/s}μtotal​=4×(1/0.040 s)=100 req/s, resulting in a stable nominal traffic intensity ρ=λμtotal=0.80\rho = \frac{\lambda}{\mu_{\text{total}}} = 0.80ρ=μtotal​λ​=0.80. However, cloud microservices are routinely disrupted by:

  • Traffic Surges: A 3×3\times3× flash crowd increases arrival rate to λburst=240 req/s\lambda_{\text{burst}} = 240\text{ req/s}λburst​=240 req/s. The traffic intensity spikes to ρ=2.40≫1.0\rho = 2.40 \gg 1.0ρ=2.40≫1.0, rapidly saturating queues.
  • Server Crashes: A crash-stop failure of 50%50\%50% of the cluster (Monline=2M_{\text{online}} = 2Monline​=2) reduces aggregate capacity to 50 req/s50\text{ req/s}50 req/s, driving traffic intensity to ρ=1.60≫1.0\rho = 1.60 \gg 1.0ρ=1.60≫1.0 even under nominal load.
  • Compound Stress: The simultaneous occurrence of a flash crowd and server dropout creates an extreme capacity mismatch (ρ=4.80\rho = 4.80ρ=4.80), causing catastrophic buffer overflow and cascading timeouts.

C. The Join-Shortest-Queue (JSQ) Pathology Under Brownout

When brownout feedback controllers are deployed on individual worker instances to shed optional tasks (θ→0\theta \to 0θ→0), service times collapse from 40 ms40\text{ ms}40 ms down to Smand=10 msS_{\text{mand}} = 10\text{ ms}Smand​=10 ms—a 4×4\times4× increase in service rate.

If the cluster ingress proxy employs conventional Join-Shortest-Queue (JSQ) routing, a severe control-balancer pathology arises:

  1. A worker that degrades (θw→0\theta_w \to 0θw​→0) completes requests four times faster than its peers, emptying its buffer rapidly.
  2. JSQ inspects queue depths (qwq_wqw​) and perceives the degraded worker as having the most available capacity.
  3. JSQ directs an overwhelming flood of incoming traffic onto the degraded worker.
  4. Conversely, healthier workers operating at higher fidelity (θ≈1.0\theta \approx 1.0θ≈1.0) process requests more slowly (40 ms40\text{ ms}40 ms), accumulate longer queues, and are starved of new traffic by JSQ.
  5. This dynamic locks the degraded worker into perpetual degradation, creates extreme load imbalance across the cluster (J≈0.61J \approx 0.61J≈0.61), and severely impedes the cluster's ability to restore healthy operational baselines when the external shock subsides.

D. Research Objectives

To overcome this fundamental challenge, this research pursues the following explicit objectives:

  1. Discrete-Event Simulation Formulation: Formulate and implement a high-fidelity, deterministic discrete-event simulation framework that models multi-worker queuing networks, dual-stage execution, client timeouts, and dynamic failure injection with multi-stream pseudo-random number generator (PRNG) isolation.
  2. Velocity-Form Feedback Controller Design: Develop and validate a discrete velocity-form Proportional-Integral (PI) brownout controller incorporating intrinsic anti-windup clamping, insufficient-sample hold logic, and derivative kick suppression during telemetry resumption.
  3. Brownout-Aware Load Balancing (BALB) Formulation: Design a multi-attribute routing algorithm that balances dimmer elasticity (θ\thetaθ), normalized queue backlog (q/Qmax⁡q / Q_{\max}q/Qmax​), and cumulative CPU utilization (UUU), incorporating dynamic anti-overloading bounds and soft-overload fallbacks.
  4. Three-Way Ablation Evaluation: Execute a pre-registered experimental matrix isolating the baseline (CFG-A), brownout control alone (CFG-B), and full brownout-aware load balancing (CFG-C) across four standardized stress scenarios.
  5. Recovery Dynamics and Trade-Off Characterization: Formulate an empirical, nominal-referenced recovery criterion (DEC-010) to quantify post-restoration recovery speed without relying on unachievable static dimmer thresholds, and rigorously evaluate the fundamental trade-off between workload distribution fairness (JJJ) and service fidelity (FFF).

III. RESEARCH CONTRIBUTIONS

The primary scientific and engineering contributions of this work are as follows:

  1. Velocity-Form Discrete PI Brownout Controller with Intrinsic Anti-Windup: We adapt the brownout control concept of Klein et al. [2] into a mathematically rigorous velocity-form discrete PI controller. By computing candidates from the clamped output of the previous step rather than an unbounded accumulator, our formulation eliminates integral windup delays without requiring artificial heuristic anti-windup resets. Furthermore, we introduce an insufficient-sample hold mechanism and derivative-state re-initialization that prevents controller destabilization during low-traffic sample starvation.
  2. Brownout-Aware Load Balancing (BALB) Scoring Algorithm: We design a composite dispatching algorithm for cluster ingress proxies. Unlike conventional JSQ or purely queue-based heuristics, BALB calculates a multi-attribute routing score:
Scorew(t)=α⋅θw(t)−β⋅(qw(t)Qmax⁡)−γ⋅Uw(t)Score_w(t) = \alpha \cdot \theta_w(t) - \beta \cdot \left(\frac{q_w(t)}{Q_{\max}}\right) - \gamma \cdot U_w(t)Scorew​(t)=α⋅θw​(t)−β⋅(Qmax​qw​(t)​)−γ⋅Uw​(t)
(3)

BALB decouples forward-looking buffer backlog risk (q/Qmax⁡q / Q_{\max}q/Qmax​) from historical processor utilization (UUU), scales an anti-overload penalty to prevent high-dimmer queue saturation, and introduces an autonomic soft-overload fallback that disables dimmer incentives when aggregate cluster buffers exceed 80%80\%80%. 3. Empirical Characterization of the Fairness–Fidelity Trade-Off: Through rigorous 360-run ablation experiments, we demonstrate that BALB resolves the pathological load skew of Join-Shortest-Queue under brownout, increasing Jain's fairness index from J≈0.65J \approx 0.65J≈0.65 to J≥0.985J \ge 0.985J≥0.985 (p<10−8p < 10^{-8}p<10−8). Crucially, our empirical analysis reveals that this equity is achieved through an inherent architectural trade-off: to prevent non-degraded instances from suffering queue-induced latency violations, BALB routes traffic to degraded nodes, causing a larger fraction of workers to operate at reduced dimmers and lowering cluster service fidelity (FFF) by 11.411.411.4 to 15.915.915.9 percentage points (p<10−38p < 10^{-38}p<10−38). 4. Nominal-Referenced Recovery Methodology (DEC-010): We identify an operational limitation in evaluating post-repair recovery against arbitrary static dimmer thresholds (such as θˉ≥0.95\bar{\theta} \ge 0.95θˉ≥0.95). In multi-server queueing systems operating under nominal load and tight latency setpoints (rtarget=80 msr_{\text{target}} = 80\text{ ms}rtarget​=80 ms), the closed-loop feedback controller naturally stabilizes at an equilibrium dimmer well below unity (θnom∗∈[0.05,0.55]\theta_{\text{nom}}^* \in [0.05, 0.55]θnom∗​∈[0.05,0.55]) to enforce response latency targets. Consequently, evaluating recovery against an unachievable static threshold near 1.01.01.0 results in artificial right-censoring. We formulate and implement DEC-010, deriving empirical, seed- and worker-specific nominal references from unperturbed stationary runs, and show that BALB accelerates post-restoration recovery by over 2×2\times2× (p<4.1×10−5p < 4.1 \times 10^{-5}p<4.1×10−5). We accompany this with full methodological disclosure regarding right-censoring horizon substitution. 5. Deterministic Multi-Stream Discrete-Event Simulation Framework: We develop and release a fully reproducible, open-source discrete-event simulation engine in Python (SimPy). By architecting five isolated PRNG sub-streams (Arrivals, Mandatory Service, Optional Service, Bernoulli Execution Draw, Failure Injection) and pre-associating attributes with immutable request tuples, our framework guarantees 100%100\%100% matched request arrival sequences and processing requirements across all three configurations, eliminating stochastic random stream desynchronization.

A. Cloud Resilience Paradigms and the Resilinets Model

The conceptual foundation of resilience in networked and computing systems stems from Laprie [6], who defined resilience as the persistence of dependability when facing changes. Sterbenz et al. [4] formalized this into the Resilinets architecture, establishing that resilience requires both Trustworthiness (reliability, availability, maintainability) and Challenge Tolerance (survivability, fault tolerance, traffic tolerance, and graceful degradation).

Central to the Resilinets model is the D2R2+DRD^2R^2 + DRD2R2+DR operational cycle:

  • Defend: Implementing proactive measures to resist adverse events.
  • Detect: Monitoring system state to recognize anomalies and SLA degradation.
  • Remediate: Dynamically mitigating the impact of faults during active shocks.
  • Recover: Restoring the system to nominal, healthy steady-state operation.
  • Diagnose & Refine: Analyzing post-incident data to adjust system parameters for future resilience.

Welsh and Benkhelifa [1] comprehensively reviewed resilience techniques across data center infrastructure, storage redundancy, hypervisor virtualization, cloud management, and service orchestration. Under their taxonomy, CloudRescue operates at the Cloud Management and Service Layer, addressing traffic tolerance and graceful degradation within the Remediate and Recover phases of the D2R2+DRD^2R^2 + DRD2R2+DR paradigm.

B. Critique of Redundancy and Reactive Auto-Scaling

A recurring finding in the Welsh and Benkhelifa [1] survey is that conventional cloud architectures excessively rely on hardware and data replication. While physical redundancy is effective against isolated hardware crashes, it incurs severe economic and operational costs:

  • Resource Inefficiency: Maintaining hot-standby instances that sit idle under nominal conditions inflates infrastructure expenditures and energy consumption.
  • Vulnerability to Correlated Shocks: Physical redundancy fails to mitigate demand-side traffic surges (flash crowds), where all replicas simultaneously experience overload.
  • Auto-Scaling Latency Gaps: Reactive elasticity frameworks rely on threshold monitoring. As highlighted by Cartlidge and Sriram [5] and surveyed by Welsh and Benkhelifa [1], provisioning additional compute instances incurs substantial scheduling, instantiation, and runtime initialization delays. During this transient provisioning gap, congested microservice instances can experience severe queue saturation and cascading timeouts.

These limitations motivate the necessity of software-level autonomic adaptation mechanisms that operate instantaneously under existing, constrained resources without relying on hardware expansion.

C. Brownout-Based Graceful Degradation

To achieve instantaneous capacity modulation, Klein et al. [2] introduced the brownout programming paradigm. Inspired by control theory in cyber-physical systems, brownout embeds self-adaptation directly into application runtimes. By decomposing requests into mandatory base operations and optional enhancements, brownout introduces a dynamic control variable—the dimmer (θ\thetaθ)—representing the probability that an admitted request will execute optional logic.

In their foundational work, Klein et al. [2] demonstrated brownout using a discrete Proportional-Integral (PI) feedback controller deployed on a single web server instance hosting the Rubis benchmark on lighttpd. The controller dynamically adjusted θ\thetaθ based on monitored response times, successfully preventing server crashes during synthetic traffic surges. Tomas and Tordsson [8] extended brownout principles to cloud overbooking, showing that brownout allows cloud providers to safely overcommit physical compute capacity while maintaining SLA compliance.

In subsequent research, Klein et al. [3] addressed the multi-server challenge by combining brownout-enabled servers with load balancing heuristics. They highlighted that conventional load balancers (such as round-robin or shortest queue) conflict with local controllers, proposing heuristics that route traffic based on dimmer values.

A. Multi-Stream PRNG Reproducibility Architecture

In stochastic simulation studies comparing control strategies, random number synchronization is critical. Under conventional simulation architectures, if a brownout controller bypasses an optional task for request kkk, the simulator draws fewer random numbers than a baseline system that executes optional logic. Consequently, subsequent request arrival timestamps and processing durations become desynchronized between configurations, confounding treatment effects with stochastic variance.

To eliminate random stream divergence, CloudRescue implements a multi-stream pseudorandom number generator (PRNG) architecture using Python's numpy.random.Generator initialized from independent PCG64 bit-generator streams derived from a master seed SSS:

  1. Stream 1 (Arrival Schedule): Generates inter-arrival durations Δtk\Delta t_kΔtk​ governing the Poisson arrival process.
  2. Stream 2 (Mandatory Processing): Generates mandatory execution times Smand,k∼Exp(μmand=0.100 ms−1)S_{\text{mand}, k} \sim \text{Exp}(\mu_{\text{mand}} = 0.100\text{ ms}^{-1})Smand,k​∼Exp(μmand​=0.100 ms−1).
  3. Stream 3 (Optional Processing): Generates optional execution times Sopt,k∼Exp(μopt=0.0333 ms−1)S_{\text{opt}, k} \sim \text{Exp}(\mu_{\text{opt}} = 0.0333\text{ ms}^{-1})Sopt,k​∼Exp(μopt​=0.0333 ms−1).
  4. Stream 4 (Optional Execution Draw): Generates uniform random variables Uopt,k∼Uniform(0.0,1.0)U_{\text{opt}, k} \sim \text{Uniform}(0.0, 1.0)Uopt,k​∼Uniform(0.0,1.0).
  5. Stream 5 (Failure Injector): Generates hardware failure schedules and crash timestamps.

Prior to simulation execution, all request entities are pre-generated as immutable tuples:

Requestk=(k,tarrive,k,Smand,k,Sopt,k,Uopt,k,Ttimeout)\text{Request}_k = \left( k, t_{\text{arrive}, k}, S_{\text{mand}, k}, S_{\text{opt}, k}, U_{\text{opt}, k}, T_{\text{timeout}} \right)Requestk​=(k,tarrive,k​,Smand,k​,Sopt,k​,Uopt,k​,Ttimeout​)
(4)

Instantaneous Optional Execution Decision:

When request kkk finishes its mandatory execution stage on worker www at timestamp tmand_endt_{\text{mand\_end}}tmand_end​, worker www evaluates its instantaneous dimmer state θw(tmand_end)\theta_w(t_{\text{mand\_end}})θw​(tmand_end​):

Execution Decision={Execute Stage 2 for duration Sopt,kif Uopt,k≤θw(tmand_end)Bypass Stage 2 immediatelyif Uopt,k>θw(tmand_end)\text{Execution Decision} = \begin{cases} \text{Execute Stage 2 for duration } S_{\text{opt}, k} & \text{if } U_{\text{opt}, k} \le \theta_w(t_{\text{mand\_end}}) \\ \text{Bypass Stage 2 immediately} & \text{if } U_{\text{opt}, k} > \theta_w(t_{\text{mand\_end}}) \end{cases}Execution Decision={Execute Stage 2 for duration Sopt,k​Bypass Stage 2 immediately​if Uopt,k​≤θw​(tmand_end​)if Uopt,k​>θw​(tmand_end​)​
(5)

Because Sopt,kS_{\text{opt}, k}Sopt,k​ and Uopt,kU_{\text{opt}, k}Uopt,k​ are pre-computed attributes of the request tuple, bypassing optional execution draws zero additional random numbers. Thus, arrival sequences and service requirements for all future requests remain bit-for-bit identical across all configurations under the same seed.

B. Velocity-Form Discrete PI Brownout Controller

Each worker instance www executes an autonomous periodic feedback controller process invoked every Δtctrl=1.0 s\Delta t_{\text{ctrl}} = 1.0\text{ s}Δtctrl​=1.0 s.

Error Formulation and Sign Convention:

Let r^95,w(t)\hat{r}_{95, w}(t)r^95,w​(t) denote the empirical 95th-percentile response latency of requests completed on worker www during the preceding interval [t−Δtctrl,t][t - \Delta t_{\text{ctrl}}, t][t−Δtctrl​,t]. The control error ew(t)e_w(t)ew​(t) is defined as:

ew(t)=rtarget−r^95,w(t)e_w(t) = r_{\text{target}} - \hat{r}_{95, w}(t)ew​(t)=rtarget​−r^95,w​(t)
(6)

Where rtarget=80.0 msr_{\text{target}} = 80.0\text{ ms}rtarget​=80.0 ms represents the controller setpoint, chosen with a 20.0 ms20.0\text{ ms}20.0 ms safety margin below the SLA threshold (rSLA=100.0 msr_{\text{SLA}} = 100.0\text{ ms}rSLA​=100.0 ms). Under this sign convention:

  • Overload Condition (r^95,w(t)>rtarget\hat{r}_{95, w}(t) > r_{\text{target}}r^95,w​(t)>rtarget​): ew(t)<0e_w(t) < 0ew​(t)<0 (negative error drives dimmer downward).
  • Underload Condition (r^95,w(t)≤rtarget\hat{r}_{95, w}(t) \le r_{\text{target}}r^95,w​(t)≤rtarget​): ew(t)≥0e_w(t) \ge 0ew​(t)≥0 (positive error drives dimmer upward toward full fidelity).

Handling Insufficient Data and Telemetry Resumption:

If the number of completed requests during the control interval is below Nmin_ctrl=5N_{\text{min\_ctrl}} = 5Nmin_ctrl​=5, latency cannot be statistically estimated:

  1. The PI mathematical update is skipped entirely.
  2. The dimmer is held constant: θw(t)=θw(t−Δtctrl)\theta_w(t) = \theta_w(t - \Delta t_{\text{ctrl}})θw​(t)=θw​(t−Δtctrl​).
  3. Queue Stall Detection: If sample count is below Nmin_ctrlN_{\text{min\_ctrl}}Nmin_ctrl​ but the worker queue is non-empty (qw(t)>0q_w(t) > 0qw​(t)>0) and the head-of-line request waiting time exceeds rtargetr_{\text{target}}rtarget​, the controller identifies queue starvation and decrements the dimmer by δstall=0.05\delta_{\text{stall}} = 0.05δstall​=0.05 to stimulate throughput.
  4. State Resumption Without Derivative Kick: When valid measurements resume at a later tick tresumet_{\text{resume}}tresume​, the previous error is re-initialized (ew,prev←ew(tresume)e_{w, \text{prev}} \leftarrow e_w(t_{\text{resume}})ew,prev​←ew​(tresume​)), ensuring that the proportional difference term evaluates to zero on the initial resumption step, eliminating artificial derivative kicks.

Recurrence and Intrinsic Anti-Windup Clamping:

The velocity-form discrete PI update calculates the incremental dimmer change:

Δθw(t)=Kp(ew(t)−ew(t−Δtctrl))+Ki⋅ew(t)⋅Δtctrl\Delta \theta_w(t) = K_p \left( e_w(t) - e_w(t - \Delta t_{\text{ctrl}}) \right) + K_i \cdot e_w(t) \cdot \Delta t_{\text{ctrl}}Δθw​(t)=Kp​(ew​(t)−ew​(t−Δtctrl​))+Ki​⋅ew​(t)⋅Δtctrl​
(7)
θcand,w(t)=θw(t−Δtctrl)+Δθw(t)\theta_{\text{cand}, w}(t) = \theta_w(t - \Delta t_{\text{ctrl}}) + \Delta \theta_w(t)θcand,w​(t)=θw​(t−Δtctrl​)+Δθw​(t)
(8)

Where proportional gain Kp=0.5K_p = 0.5Kp​=0.5 and integral gain Ki=0.1 s−1K_i = 0.1\text{ s}^{-1}Ki​=0.1 s−1.

The candidate value is clamped to the physical probability interval:

θw(t)=clamp(θcand,w(t),θmin,θmax)=max⁡(0.0,min⁡(1.0,θcand,w(t)))\theta_w(t) = \text{clamp}\left( \theta_{\text{cand}, w}(t), \theta_{\text{min}}, \theta_{\text{max}} \right) = \max\left( 0.0, \min\left( 1.0, \theta_{\text{cand}, w}(t) \right) \right)θw​(t)=clamp(θcand,w​(t),θmin​,θmax​)=max(0.0,min(1.0,θcand,w​(t)))
(9)

Intrinsic Anti-Windup Mechanics: Because subsequent control steps calculate θcand,w(t+Δtctrl)\theta_{\text{cand}, w}(t + \Delta t_{\text{ctrl}})θcand,w​(t+Δtctrl​) directly from the clamped output θw(t)\theta_w(t)θw​(t) rather than an unconstrained internal accumulator, no phantom integral state accumulates beyond the physical boundaries [0.0,1.0][0.0, 1.0][0.0,1.0]. The instant control error reverses sign (ew(t)>0e_w(t) > 0ew​(t)>0), θw(t)\theta_w(t)θw​(t) immediately begins recovering upward with zero unwinding lag.

C. Brownout-Aware Load Balancing (BALB) Algorithm

In CFG-C, the ingress load balancer dynamically evaluates all operational worker instances for each arriving request.

Mathematical Dispatch Score:

The utility score for operational worker www at arrival timestamp ttt is formulated as:

Scorew(t)=α⋅θw(t)−β⋅(qw(t)Qmax⁡)−γ⋅Uw(t)Score_w(t) = \alpha \cdot \theta_w(t) - \beta \cdot \left(\frac{q_w(t)}{Q_{\max}}\right) - \gamma \cdot U_w(t)Scorew​(t)=α⋅θw​(t)−β⋅(Qmax​qw​(t)​)−γ⋅Uw​(t)
(10)

Where:

  • θw(t)∈[0.0,1.0]\theta_w(t) \in [0.0, 1.0]θw​(t)∈[0.0,1.0] is the instantaneous dimmer of worker www, incentivizing routing toward high-fidelity instances.
  • qw(t)∈[0,Qmax⁡]q_w(t) \in [0, Q_{\max}]qw​(t)∈[0,Qmax​] is the instantaneous queue depth of worker www, normalized by buffer capacity Qmax⁡=50Q_{\max} = 50Qmax​=50, serving as a forward-looking indicator of queuing delay and buffer overflow risk.
  • Uw(t)∈[0.0,1.0]U_w(t) \in [0.0, 1.0]Uw​(t)∈[0.0,1.0] is the cumulative CPU utilization of worker www up to the decision timestamp, defined as operational busy time divided by operational uptime (Tbusy,w/Toperational,wT_{\text{busy}, w} / T_{\text{operational}, w}Tbusy,w​/Toperational,w​), reflecting historical processing load.
  • α,β,γ\alpha, \beta, \gammaα,β,γ are non-negative weighting coefficients. In default operation, α=1.0\alpha = 1.0α=1.0, β=1.0\beta = 1.0β=1.0, and γ=0.5\gamma = 0.5γ=0.5.

Anti-Overload Penalty and Soft-Overload Fallback:

  1. Dynamic Queue Backlog Suppression: Because qwQmax⁡\frac{q_w}{Q_{\max}}Qmax​qw​​ scales continuously with queue occupancy, any attempt to continually route requests to a high-dimmer worker (θw=1.0\theta_w = 1.0θw​=1.0) rapidly increases the penalty term −β(qwQmax⁡)-\beta \left(\frac{q_w}{Q_{\max}}\right)−β(Qmax​qw​​), automatically redirecting traffic before the buffer overflows.
  2. Soft-Overload Fallback Policy: If all operational workers experience severe congestion such that qw(t)≥Qsoftq_w(t) \ge Q_{\text{soft}}qw​(t)≥Qsoft​ (where Qsoft=0.8⋅Qmax⁡=40 requestsQ_{\text{soft}} = 0.8 \cdot Q_{\max} = 40\text{ requests}Qsoft​=0.8⋅Qmax​=40 requests), dimmer incentives become dangerous. In this regime, BALB autonomic fallbacks by setting α=0\alpha = 0α=0:
Scorewfallback(t)=−β⋅(qw(t)Qmax⁡)−γ⋅Uw(t)Score_w^{\text{fallback}}(t) = - \beta \cdot \left(\frac{q_w(t)}{Q_{\max}}\right) - \gamma \cdot U_w(t)Scorewfallback​(t)=−β⋅(Qmax​qw​(t)​)−γ⋅Uw​(t)
(11)

This immediately eliminates feature-fidelity incentives, prioritizing buffer survival and workload draining across all workers. 3. Crash Masking: Crashed instances are flagged by the failure detector and assigned Scorew=−∞Score_w = -\inftyScorew​=−∞, excluding them from routing decisions.

The complete BALB dispatch logic is summarized in Algorithm 1.

Algorithm 1: Brownout-Aware Load Balancing (BALB) Request Dispatching
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Input  : Arriving Request k at timestamp t;
         Worker cluster W = {0, 1, ..., M-1};
         Parameters alpha, beta, gamma, Q_max, Q_soft = 0.8 * Q_max.
Output : Target worker index w_star for dispatch.

1  W_operational <- { w in W | worker w is online and not crashed }
2  if W_operational is empty then
3      Record client connection rejection (Cluster Outage);
4      return null;
5  end

6  // Check cluster-wide soft overload threshold
7  all_congested <- true
8  for each w in W_operational do
9      if q_w(t) < Q_soft then
10         all_congested <- false;
11         break;
12     end
13 end

14 // Calculate routing scores
15 effective_alpha <- if all_congested then 0.0 else alpha
16 max_score <- -infinity
17 candidates <- []

18 for each w in W_operational do
19     // Calculate normalized metrics
20     norm_q <- q_w(t) / Q_max
21     score_w <- (effective_alpha * theta_w(t)) - (beta * norm_q) - (gamma * U_w(t))
22     
23     if score_w > max_score then
24         max_score <- score_w;
25         candidates <- [ w ];
26     else if score_w == max_score then
27         Append w to candidates;
28     end
29 end

30 // Break ties deterministically or uniformly
31 w_star <- SelectFirstOrUniform(candidates)
32 Dispatch Request k to Worker w_star;
33 return w_star;
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

D. Experimental Configurations for Three-Way Ablation

To scientifically evaluate CloudRescue, we establish three comparative configurations:

  1. Configuration A (CFG-A, Unmanaged Baseline): Represents conventional cloud service deployments without graceful degradation. Workers operate with fixed full fidelity (θ≡1.0\theta \equiv 1.0θ≡1.0), executing both mandatory and optional components for all admitted requests. Routing is performed using conventional Join-Shortest-Queue (JSQ), dispatching to the operational worker with the minimum current buffer depth (qwq_wqw​).
  2. Configuration B (CFG-B, Brownout Only): Deploys the velocity-form discrete PI brownout controller on each worker instance, allowing workers to dynamically shed optional tasks (θw(t)∈[0,1]\theta_w(t) \in [0, 1]θw​(t)∈[0,1]). However, cluster routing remains unmanaged, employing conventional Join-Shortest-Queue (JSQ). This configuration cleanly isolates the impact of local graceful degradation while exposing the pathological control-balancer interaction.
  3. Configuration C (CFG-C, Full CloudRescue): Combines the velocity-form discrete PI brownout feedback controller on worker instances with Brownout-Aware Load Balancing (BALB) at the ingress proxy. Comparing CFG-C directly against CFG-B isolates the exact incremental contribution of brownout-aware routing over local brownout control alone.

VI. EXPERIMENTAL METHODOLOGY

A. Simulation Environment and Discrete-Event Model

CloudRescue is evaluated through a high-fidelity, deterministic discrete-event simulation framework implemented in Python 3.10 using the simpy discrete-event simulation kernel [9]. While physical multi-node cloud testbeds provide operational realism, they introduce non-deterministic confounders—such as hypervisor scheduling jitter, background OS kernel interrupts, virtualized NIC driver latency variations, and uncontrollable garbage collection pauses—that obscure the core dynamical interactions between feedback controllers and load balancers.

Discrete-event simulation provides a rigorous, controlled environment where every request arrival, queue transition, CPU execution stage, and controller update is scheduled as an explicit discrete event on an event timeline with microsecond temporal resolution (1000 ms=1,000,000 μs1000\text{ ms} = 1,000,000\text{ }\mu\text{s}1000 ms=1,000,000 μs). The simulation engine strictly manages state transitions across five discrete life-cycle stages:

  1. REQUEST_ARRIVAL: Ingress load balancer receives an arriving request tuple and evaluates the operational worker pool.
  2. WORKER_ENQUEUE: The target worker either rejects the request (DROP_QUEUE_FULL) if queue depth satisfies qw(t)≥Qmax⁡q_w(t) \ge Q_{\max}qw​(t)≥Qmax​, or appends the request to its FIFO queue.
  3. SERVICE_STAGE_1: When the request reaches the head of the queue, the worker evaluates elapsed waiting time Wk=tstart,k−tarrive,kW_k = t_{\text{start}, k} - t_{\text{arrive}, k}Wk​=tstart,k​−tarrive,k​. If Wk>TtimeoutW_k > T_{\text{timeout}}Wk​>Ttimeout​, the request is aborted (DROP_TIMEOUT). Otherwise, the worker acquires the single CPU resource and executes mandatory logic for duration Smand,kS_{\text{mand}, k}Smand,k​.
  4. SERVICE_STAGE_2: Upon completing Stage 1, the worker checks its instantaneous dimmer θw(t)\theta_w(t)θw​(t) against the pre-assigned random variable Uopt,kU_{\text{opt}, k}Uopt,k​. If Uopt,k≤θw(t)U_{\text{opt}, k} \le \theta_w(t)Uopt,k​≤θw​(t), Stage 2 executes for duration Sopt,kS_{\text{opt}, k}Sopt,k​; otherwise, Stage 2 is bypassed immediately.
  5. REQUEST_COMPLETED: The CPU is released, the response is delivered, and end-to-end response latency Lk=tcompleted,k−tarrive,kL_k = t_{\text{completed}, k} - t_{\text{arrive}, k}Lk​=tcompleted,k​−tarrive,k​ is logged. If Lk>rSLAL_k > r_{\text{SLA}}Lk​>rSLA​, the request is flagged as a latency SLA violation.

B. Cluster Topology and Workload Model

The modeled topology comprises a centralized ingress proxy fronting a cluster of M=4M = 4M=4 independent worker instances (w∈{0,1,2,3}w \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}w∈{0,1,2,3}). The proxy processes incoming requests instantaneously with zero buffer holding delay, dispatching each request immediately to one of the worker nodes according to the active routing policy.

Each worker manages a dedicated finite FIFO buffer with maximum capacity Qmax⁡=50 requestsQ_{\max} = 50\text{ requests}Qmax​=50 requests. Client HTTP connections enforce an application timeout deadline Ttimeout=200.0 msT_{\text{timeout}} = 200.0\text{ ms}Ttimeout​=200.0 ms. The service level agreement contractually mandates a 95th-percentile response latency threshold rSLA=100.0 msr_{\text{SLA}} = 100.0\text{ ms}rSLA​=100.0 ms. To maintain an operational safety buffer against latency spikes, local PI feedback controllers target a conservative setpoint rtarget=80.0 msr_{\text{target}} = 80.0\text{ ms}rtarget​=80.0 ms. Local controllers execute periodically with control interval Δtctrl=1.0 s\Delta t_{\text{ctrl}} = 1.0\text{ s}Δtctrl​=1.0 s, requiring a minimum sample count Nmin_ctrl=5 requestsN_{\text{min\_ctrl}} = 5\text{ requests}Nmin_ctrl​=5 requests to compute valid empirical latencies, with proportional gain Kp=0.5K_p = 0.5Kp​=0.5, integral gain Ki=0.1 s−1K_i = 0.1\text{ s}^{-1}Ki​=0.1 s−1, and stalled queue decrement δstall=0.05\delta_{\text{stall}} = 0.05δstall​=0.05.

C. Service Time Distributions

Request execution demands are modeled using standard Markovian exponential distributions:

  • Mandatory Logic (SmandS_{\text{mand}}Smand​): Smand,k∼Exp(μmand=0.100 ms−1)S_{\text{mand}, k} \sim \text{Exp}(\mu_{\text{mand}} = 0.100\text{ ms}^{-1})Smand,k​∼Exp(μmand​=0.100 ms−1), with mean service time E[Smand]=10.0 ms\mathbb{E}[S_{\text{mand}}] = 10.0\text{ ms}E[Smand​]=10.0 ms.
  • Optional Logic (SoptS_{\text{opt}}Sopt​): Sopt,k∼Exp(μopt=0.0333 ms−1)S_{\text{opt}, k} \sim \text{Exp}(\mu_{\text{opt}} = 0.0333\text{ ms}^{-1})Sopt,k​∼Exp(μopt​=0.0333 ms−1), with mean service time E[Sopt]=30.0 ms\mathbb{E}[S_{\text{opt}}] = 30.0\text{ ms}E[Sopt​]=30.0 ms.

Under full service fidelity (θ=1.0\theta = 1.0θ=1.0), total expected processing time per request is:

E[Sfull]=E[Smand]+E[Sopt]=10.0 ms+30.0 ms=40.0 ms\mathbb{E}[S_{\text{full}}] = \mathbb{E}[S_{\text{mand}}] + \mathbb{E}[S_{\text{opt}}] = 10.0\text{ ms} + 30.0\text{ ms} = 40.0\text{ ms}E[Sfull​]=E[Smand​]+E[Sopt​]=10.0 ms+30.0 ms=40.0 ms
(12)

Each worker provides a nominal processing service rate μw=10.040 s=25.0 req/s\mu_w = \frac{1}{0.040\text{ s}} = 25.0\text{ req/s}μw​=0.040 s1​=25.0 req/s, yielding an aggregate 4-worker cluster serving capacity of μtotal=100.0 req/s\mu_{\text{total}} = 100.0\text{ req/s}μtotal​=100.0 req/s.

Conversely, under complete brownout degradation (θ=0.0\theta = 0.0θ=0.0), optional logic is shed entirely, reducing expected processing time to:

E[Sdegraded]=E[Smand]=10.0 ms\mathbb{E}[S_{\text{degraded}}] = \mathbb{E}[S_{\text{mand}}] = 10.0\text{ ms}E[Sdegraded​]=E[Smand​]=10.0 ms
(13)

This expands individual worker service rate to μw=100.0 req/s\mu_w = 100.0\text{ req/s}μw​=100.0 req/s and aggregate cluster capacity to μtotal=400.0 req/s\mu_{\text{total}} = 400.0\text{ req/s}μtotal​=400.0 req/s, providing a fourfold expansion in transaction throughput capacity without allocating additional physical instances.

D. Multi-Stream PRNG Architecture and Paired Inputs

To enable strict Common Random Numbers (CRN) variance reduction across configurations [10], each simulation trial utilizes five independent pseudo-random number generator (PRNG) sub-streams derived from a master seed SSS:

  1. Stream 1 (Request Arrivals): Generates Poisson inter-arrival intervals Δtk∼Exp(λ(t))\Delta t_k \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda(t))Δtk​∼Exp(λ(t)).
  2. Stream 2 (Mandatory Duration): Generates mandatory execution demands Smand,k∼Exp(0.100 ms−1)S_{\text{mand}, k} \sim \text{Exp}(0.100\text{ ms}^{-1})Smand,k​∼Exp(0.100 ms−1).
  3. Stream 3 (Optional Duration): Generates optional execution demands Sopt,k∼Exp(0.0333 ms−1)S_{\text{opt}, k} \sim \text{Exp}(0.0333\text{ ms}^{-1})Sopt,k​∼Exp(0.0333 ms−1).
  4. Stream 4 (Bernoulli Dimmer Draw): Generates independent execution thresholds Uopt,k∼Uniform(0.0,1.0)U_{\text{opt}, k} \sim \text{Uniform}(0.0, 1.0)Uopt,k​∼Uniform(0.0,1.0).
  5. Stream 5 (Failure Injection): Generates hardware failure schedules and crash timestamps.

All request entities are instantiated prior to simulation execution as immutable data structures:

Requestk=(k,tarrive,k,Smand,k,Sopt,k,Uopt,k,Ttimeout)\text{Request}_k = \left( k, t_{\text{arrive}, k}, S_{\text{mand}, k}, S_{\text{opt}, k}, U_{\text{opt}, k}, T_{\text{timeout}} \right)Requestk​=(k,tarrive,k​,Smand,k​,Sopt,k​,Uopt,k​,Ttimeout​)
(14)

This decoupled pre-generation architecture guarantees that whether a worker executes or bypasses optional Stage 2, zero pseudorandom numbers are drawn from the generators during execution. Consequently, the arrival times, mandatory durations, and optional requirements of all future requests remain bit-for-bit identical across CFG-A, CFG-B, and CFG-C, eliminating stochastic input divergence.

E. Experimental Configurations (Ablation Matrix)

We define three comparative configurations to execute a clean single-variable ablation:

  • CFG-A (Unmanaged Baseline): Fixed full fidelity (θ≡1.0\theta \equiv 1.0θ≡1.0, brownout disabled) combined with conventional Join-Shortest-Queue (JSQ) routing.
  • CFG-B (Brownout Controller Alone): Autonomous velocity-form discrete PI brownout controller active on each worker (θw(t)∈[0,1]\theta_w(t) \in [0, 1]θw​(t)∈[0,1]), combined with conventional Join-Shortest-Queue (JSQ) routing.
  • CFG-C (Full CloudRescue): Autonomous velocity-form discrete PI brownout controller active on each worker (θw(t)∈[0,1]\theta_w(t) \in [0, 1]θw​(t)∈[0,1]), combined with Brownout-Aware Load Balancing (BALB) utilizing multi-attribute scoring (Scorew=αθw−βqwQmax⁡−γUwScore_w = \alpha \theta_w - \beta \frac{q_w}{Q_{\max}} - \gamma U_wScorew​=αθw​−βQmax​qw​​−γUw​), anti-overload bounds, and soft-overload fallback.

Comparing CFG-B against CFG-A isolates the localized benefit of brownout adaptation under conventional routing. Comparing CFG-C against CFG-B isolates the exact incremental contribution of brownout-aware load balancing.

F. Standardized Stress Scenarios

The cluster is evaluated across four standardized operational scenarios:

  1. At t=300.0 st = 300.0\text{ s}t=300.0 s, a sudden 3×3\times3× traffic surge elevates arrival rate to λburst=240.0 req/s\lambda_{\text{burst}} = 240.0\text{ req/s}λburst​=240.0 req/s for a duration of Δt=150.0 s\Delta t = 150.0\text{ s}Δt=150.0 s (t∈[300.0 s,450.0 s]t \in [300.0\text{ s}, 450.0\text{ s}]t∈[300.0 s,450.0 s]). At t=450.0 st = 450.0\text{ s}t=450.0 s, arrival rate abruptly returns to nominal 80.0 req/s80.0\text{ req/s}80.0 req/s for the remainder of the run (t∈[450.0 s,1000.0 s]t \in [450.0\text{ s}, 1000.0\text{ s}]t∈[450.0 s,1000.0 s]). During the surge, traffic intensity reaches ρ=240100=2.40≫1.0\rho = \frac{240}{100} = 2.40 \gg 1.0ρ=100240​=2.40≫1.0.
  3. Scenario 3 — Server Crash Failure: Inbound arrival rate remains stationary at λ=80.0 req/s\lambda = 80.0\text{ req/s}λ=80.0 req/s. At t=300.0 st = 300.0\text{ s}t=300.0 s, workers 1 and 2 experience an abrupt crash-stop failure (50%50\%50% capacity reduction, Monline=2M_{\text{online}} = 2Monline​=2) lasting until t=450.0 st = 450.0\text{ s}t=450.0 s (Δt=150.0 s\Delta t = 150.0\text{ s}Δt=150.0 s), at which point they are repaired and rejoin the cluster. During the outage, aggregate cluster capacity drops to 50.0 req/s50.0\text{ req/s}50.0 req/s, forcing traffic intensity to ρ=8050=1.60≫1.0\rho = \frac{80}{50} = 1.60 \gg 1.0ρ=5080​=1.60≫1.0.

While arrival rate surges to λburst=240.0 req/s\lambda_{\text{burst}} = 240.0\text{ req/s}λburst​=240.0 req/s, workers 1 and 2 concurrently experience a crash-stop failure from t=300.0 st = 300.0\text{ s}t=300.0 s to t=450.0 st = 450.0\text{ s}t=450.0 s. Aggregate capacity drops to 50.0 req/s50.0\text{ req/s}50.0 req/s while load triples, driving traffic intensity to an extreme peak of ρ=24050=4.80≫1.0\rho = \frac{240}{50} = 4.80 \gg 1.0ρ=50240​=4.80≫1.0.

G. Primary 360-Run Factorial Design

The primary experimental battery executes a full factorial design:

Total Primary Runs=3 Configurations×4 Scenarios×30 Matched Seeds=360 simulation executions\text{Total Primary Runs} = 3 \text{ Configurations} \times 4 \text{ Scenarios} \times 30 \text{ Matched Seeds} = \mathbf{360 \text{ simulation executions}}Total Primary Runs=3 Configurations×4 Scenarios×30 Matched Seeds=360 simulation executions
(15)

The 30 master seeds are pre-registered consecutively (S∈[1001,1030]S \in [1001, 1030]S∈[1001,1030]). Within each scenario and seed, the identical pre-generated workload stream is presented to CFG-A, CFG-B, and CFG-C, establishing a strictly paired experimental design across all 120 unique scenario-seed combinations.

H. Exploratory 144-Run BALB Sensitivity Sweep & Status

To investigate the stability of the BALB composite scoring parameters, an auxiliary multi-factor grid sweep was executed under the most challenging operating condition (Compound Stress). The sweep evaluated:

  • Dimmer weight: α∈{0.5,1.0,1.5,2.0}\alpha \in \{0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0\}α∈{0.5,1.0,1.5,2.0} (4 levels)
  • Normalized queue penalty: β∈{0.5,1.0,1.5,2.0}\beta \in \{0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0\}β∈{0.5,1.0,1.5,2.0} (4 levels)
  • CPU utilization penalty: γ∈{0.0,0.5,1.0}\gamma \in \{0.0, 0.5, 1.0\}γ∈{0.0,0.5,1.0} (3 levels)

This yields 4×4×3=48 unique parameter combinations4 \times 4 \times 3 = 48\text{ unique parameter combinations}4×4×3=48 unique parameter combinations. Each parameter cell was evaluated across n=3n = 3n=3 independent seeds (S∈{1001,1002,1003}S \in \{1001, 1002, 1003\}S∈{1001,1002,1003}), totaling:

Total Sensitivity Runs=48 cells×3 seeds=144 simulation executions\text{Total Sensitivity Runs} = 48 \text{ cells} \times 3 \text{ seeds} = \mathbf{144 \text{ simulation executions}}Total Sensitivity Runs=48 cells×3 seeds=144 simulation executions
(16)

[!NOTE] Exploratory Status and Limitations:
Because each parameter combination is evaluated over only three pseudo-random seeds (n=3n=3n=3), this sensitivity sweep is strictly exploratory. While it confirms that BALB performance is broadly stable across wide parameter ranges and validates that the default weights (α=1.0,β=1.0,γ=0.5\alpha = 1.0, \beta = 1.0, \gamma = 0.5α=1.0,β=1.0,γ=0.5) perform reliably without inducing control divergence, fine-grained differences between top-ranking cells fall within small-sample stochastic margins. Consequently, the observed configurations are not claimed as a globally proven mathematical optimum.

I. Simulation Horizon, Warmup, and Temporal Windows

  • Total Duration (TsimT_{\text{sim}}Tsim​): Each run executes for 1000.0 s1000.0\text{ s}1000.0 s (1,000,000 ms1,000,000\text{ ms}1,000,000 ms).
  • Warm-Up Window (TwarmupT_{\text{warmup}}Twarmup​): The initial 100.0 s100.0\text{ s}100.0 s (100,000 ms100,000\text{ ms}100,000 ms) interval is designated as the transient warm-up phase. All requests arriving before twarmup=100.0 st_{\text{warmup}} = 100.0\text{ s}twarmup​=100.0 s are excluded from steady-state metric calculations to eliminate pipeline initialization bias.
  • Evaluation Window: Performance metrics are computed strictly over requests arriving in the interval t∈[100.0 s,1000.0 s]t \in [100.0\text{ s}, 1000.0\text{ s}]t∈[100.0 s,1000.0 s].
  • Stress Window: Active disruptions (flash crowd burst and/or server outages) occur from tshock_start=300.0 st_{\text{shock\_start}} = 300.0\text{ s}tshock_start​=300.0 s to tshock_end=450.0 st_{\text{shock\_end}} = 450.0\text{ s}tshock_end​=450.0 s (Δt=150.0 s\Delta t = 150.0\text{ s}Δt=150.0 s).
  • Post-Restoration Window: Following server repair and traffic normalization at t=450.0 st = 450.0\text{ s}t=450.0 s, system recovery is monitored until simulation completion at t=1000.0 st = 1000.0\text{ s}t=1000.0 s, establishing a maximum observation horizon of Tcensor=550.0 sT_{\text{censor}} = 550.0\text{ s}Tcensor​=550.0 s.

J. Authoritative Metric Definitions and Mathematical Rules

All metrics are derived from discrete event logs recorded outside the warm-up window (t≥100.0 st \ge 100.0\text{ s}t≥100.0 s).

Request Populations:

  • NsubmittedN_{\text{submitted}}Nsubmitted​: Total requests arriving post-warmup (∑k1(tarrive,k≥100.0 s)\sum_k \mathbf{1}(t_{\text{arrive}, k} \ge 100.0\text{ s})∑k​1(tarrive,k​≥100.0 s)).
  • NsuccessN_{\text{success}}Nsuccess​: Total completed requests with response latency Lk≤TtimeoutL_k \le T_{\text{timeout}}Lk​≤Ttimeout​ (200.0 ms200.0\text{ ms}200.0 ms).
  • Ndrop_queueN_{\text{drop\_queue}}Ndrop_queue​: Requests rejected upon arrival due to full worker buffers (qw≥Qmax⁡q_w \ge Q_{\max}qw​≥Qmax​).
  • Ndrop_timeoutN_{\text{drop\_timeout}}Ndrop_timeout​: Requests aborted at the head of a worker queue due to waiting time Wk>TtimeoutW_k > T_{\text{timeout}}Wk​>Ttimeout​.
  • Ncrash_failedN_{\text{crash\_failed}}Ncrash_failed​: Requests in-flight or buffered on worker nodes when a crash-stop failure occurs.
  • Nlat_violN_{\text{lat\_viol}}Nlat_viol​: Successful requests whose response latency breaches the SLA threshold (Lk>100.0 msL_k > 100.0\text{ ms}Lk​>100.0 ms).

1. Request Success Rate (SrS_rSr​):

Measures system transaction completion ratio:

Sr=NsuccessNsubmitted×100%S_r = \frac{N_{\text{success}}}{N_{\text{submitted}}} \times 100\%Sr​=Nsubmitted​Nsuccess​​×100%
(17)

2. Latency SLA Violation Rate (VlatV_{\text{lat}}Vlat​) — Evaluated Over Successful Requests:

Measures latency compliance strictly among requests delivered to the client:

Vlat={Nlat_violNsuccess×100%if Nsuccess>00%if Nsuccess=0V_{\text{lat}} = \begin{cases} \frac{N_{\text{lat\_viol}}}{N_{\text{success}}} \times 100\% & \text{if } N_{\text{success}} > 0 \\ 0\% & \text{if } N_{\text{success}} = 0 \end{cases}Vlat​={Nsuccess​Nlat_viol​​×100%0%​if Nsuccess​>0if Nsuccess​=0​
(18)
  • Denominator: NsuccessN_{\text{success}}Nsuccess​ (completed requests with Lk≤200.0 msL_k \le 200.0\text{ ms}Lk​≤200.0 ms).

3. Overall SLA Failure Rate (VoverallV_{\text{overall}}Voverall​) — Evaluated Over All Submitted Requests:

Provides an end-to-end reliability measure combining unserved requests and degraded responses:

Voverall=Nlat_viol+Ndrop_timeout+Ndrop_queue+Ncrash_failedNsubmitted×100%V_{\text{overall}} = \frac{N_{\text{lat\_viol}} + N_{\text{drop\_timeout}} + N_{\text{drop\_queue}} + N_{\text{crash\_failed}}}{N_{\text{submitted}}} \times 100\%Voverall​=Nsubmitted​Nlat_viol​+Ndrop_timeout​+Ndrop_queue​+Ncrash_failed​​×100%
(19)
  • Denominator: NsubmittedN_{\text{submitted}}Nsubmitted​ (all arriving requests).

Mathematical Non-Additivity of VlatV_{\text{lat}}Vlat​ and VoverallV_{\text{overall}}Voverall​:

A critical methodological requirement is recognizing that VlatV_{\text{lat}}Vlat​ and VoverallV_{\text{overall}}Voverall​ cannot be directly summed because they possess mathematically distinct denominators (NsuccessN_{\text{success}}Nsuccess​ versus NsubmittedN_{\text{submitted}}Nsubmitted​). The exact formulation connecting the two metrics is:

Voverall=(Nlat_violNsubmitted)+Ddrop_rateV_{\text{overall}} = \left(\frac{N_{\text{lat\_viol}}}{N_{\text{submitted}}}\right) + D_{\text{drop\_rate}}Voverall​=(Nsubmitted​Nlat_viol​​)+Ddrop_rate​
(20)

Multiplying and dividing the first term by NsuccessN_{\text{success}}Nsuccess​:

Voverall=(Nlat_violNsuccess)⋅(NsuccessNsubmitted)+Ddrop_rate=Vlat⋅(Sr100)+Ddrop_rateV_{\text{overall}} = \left(\frac{N_{\text{lat\_viol}}}{N_{\text{success}}}\right) \cdot \left(\frac{N_{\text{success}}}{N_{\text{submitted}}}\right) + D_{\text{drop\_rate}} = V_{\text{lat}} \cdot \left(\frac{S_r}{100}\right) + D_{\text{drop\_rate}}Voverall​=(Nsuccess​Nlat_viol​​)⋅(Nsubmitted​Nsuccess​​)+Ddrop_rate​=Vlat​⋅(100Sr​​)+Ddrop_rate​
(21)

Where Ddrop_rate=Ndrop_timeout+Ndrop_queue+Ncrash_failedNsubmitted×100%D_{\text{drop\_rate}} = \frac{N_{\text{drop\_timeout}} + N_{\text{drop\_queue}} + N_{\text{crash\_failed}}}{N_{\text{submitted}}} \times 100\%Ddrop_rate​=Nsubmitted​Ndrop_timeout​+Ndrop_queue​+Ncrash_failed​​×100%. Unweighted summation of VlatV_{\text{lat}}Vlat​ and drop rate produces an erroneous, inflated quantity that violates basic probability axioms.

4. Latency Statistics (P95P_{95}P95​ and Lˉ\bar{L}Lˉ):

  • Mean Response Latency (Lˉ\bar{L}Lˉ): Arithmetic mean of LkL_kLk​ over all successful requests (Ssuccess\mathcal{S}_{\text{success}}Ssuccess​).
  • 95th-Percentile Latency (P95P_{95}P95​): Empirical 95th percentile computed via linear rank interpolation over Ssuccess\mathcal{S}_{\text{success}}Ssuccess​.

5. Service Fidelity (FFF) — Strict Subset Formulation:

Measures the proportion of successful transactions delivered with optional enhancements:

F={Nfull_fidelityNsuccess×100%if Nsuccess>00%if Nsuccess=0F = \begin{cases} \frac{N_{\text{full\_fidelity}}}{N_{\text{success}}} \times 100\% & \text{if } N_{\text{success}} > 0 \\ 0\% & \text{if } N_{\text{success}} = 0 \end{cases}F={Nsuccess​Nfull_fidelity​​×100%0%​if Nsuccess​>0if Nsuccess​=0​
(22)

Because only successfully delivered requests can execute optional features, Sfull_fidelity⊆Ssuccess\mathcal{S}_{\text{full\_fidelity}} \subseteq \mathcal{S}_{\text{success}}Sfull_fidelity​⊆Ssuccess​ holds strictly, guaranteeing 0%≤F≤100%0\% \le F \le 100\%0%≤F≤100%. For baseline CFG-A, F≡100.00%F \equiv 100.00\%F≡100.00% by definition.

6. Jain's Fairness Index (JJJ):

Measures the parity of workload dispatching across active worker instances [11]:

J=(∑w∈MactiveCw)2∣Mactive∣⋅∑w∈MactiveCw2J = \frac{\left(\sum_{w \in M_{\text{active}}} C_w\right)^2}{|M_{\text{active}}| \cdot \sum_{w \in M_{\text{active}}} C_w^2}J=∣Mactive​∣⋅∑w∈Mactive​​Cw2​(∑w∈Mactive​​Cw​)2​
(23)

Where CwC_wCw​ is the count of requests dispatched to worker www post-warmup.

  • Operational Worker Rule: In Nominal and Flash Crowd scenarios, all four workers operate without outage (Mactive={0,1,2,3}M_{\text{active}} = \{0, 1, 2, 3\}Mactive​={0,1,2,3}, ∣Mactive∣=4|M_{\text{active}}| = 4∣Mactive​∣=4). In Server Crash and Compound Stress scenarios, workers 1 and 2 experience scheduled downtime (t∈[300,450 s]t \in [300, 450\text{ s}]t∈[300,450 s]). To prevent scheduled hardware downtime from being misclassified as load-balancer routing bias, JJJ is evaluated strictly across the zero-downtime operational pool Mactive={0,3}M_{\text{active}} = \{0, 3\}Mactive​={0,3} (∣Mactive∣=2|M_{\text{active}}| = 2∣Mactive​∣=2).

7) Recovery Dynamics: Adaptation vs. Post-Restoration Recovery:

We formally decouple two distinct recovery phenomena:

  • Adaptation Recovery Time (TadaptT_{\text{adapt}}Tadapt​) During Active Stress: Measures how quickly the system stabilizes response times while the disruption is actively ongoing. Defined as the elapsed time from shock onset (tshock_start=300.0 st_{\text{shock\_start}} = 300.0\text{ s}tshock_start​=300.0 s) until the rolling 95th-percentile response latency drops below rSLA=100.0 msr_{\text{SLA}} = 100.0\text{ ms}rSLA​=100.0 ms:
Tadapt=tadapted−300.0 sT_{\text{adapt}} = t_{\text{adapted}} - 300.0\text{ s}Tadapt​=tadapted​−300.0 s
(24)

Where tadaptedt_{\text{adapted}}tadapted​ is the earliest timestamp where rolling r^95(t)≤100.0 ms\hat{r}_{95}(t) \le 100.0\text{ ms}r^95​(t)≤100.0 ms holds continuously for tstable=3.0 st_{\text{stable}} = 3.0\text{ s}tstable​=3.0 s (3×Δtctrl3\times \Delta t_{\text{ctrl}}3×Δtctrl​), evaluated across a Wrec=10.0 sW_{\text{rec}} = 10.0\text{ s}Wrec​=10.0 s sliding window requiring at least Nrec_min=20 completed requestsN_{\text{rec\_min}} = 20\text{ completed requests}Nrec_min​=20 completed requests.

  • Post-Restoration Recovery Time (TrestoreT_{\text{restore}}Trestore​) After Server Repair: Measures the elapsed time required to return to healthy nominal steady state following server repair at trepair=450.0 st_{\text{repair}} = 450.0\text{ s}trepair​=450.0 s:
Trestore=trestored−450.0 sT_{\text{restore}} = t_{\text{restored}} - 450.0\text{ s}Trestore​=trestored​−450.0 s
(25)

In accordance with decision DEC-010, recovery cannot be judged against an arbitrary static threshold (e.g., θˉ≥0.95\bar{\theta} \ge 0.95θˉ≥0.95), because steady-state nominal operation under tight latency targets stabilizes at lower dimmers. Post-restoration recovery is achieved at the earliest timestamp t≥450.0 st \ge 450.0\text{ s}t≥450.0 s satisfying:

  1. Both restored workers achieve at least 95%95\%95% of their configuration-, seed-, and worker-specific nominal steady-state reference:
θw(t)≥0.95⋅θnom∗(c,s,w)∀w∈{1,2}\theta_w(t) \ge 0.95 \cdot \theta_{\text{nom}}^*(c, s, w) \quad \forall w \in \{1, 2\}θw​(t)≥0.95⋅θnom∗​(c,s,w)∀w∈{1,2}
(26)
 Where <span data-inline-math="313"></span> is derived from the steady-state nominal window <span data-inline-math="314"></span> of the corresponding nominal run for configuration <span data-inline-math="315"></span>, seed <span data-inline-math="316"></span>, and worker <span data-inline-math="317"></span>. Across the 2 brownout configurations (`CFG-B`, `CFG-C`), 30 seeds, and 2 restored workers, exactly <span data-inline-math="318"></span> are evaluated.
  1. Rolling cluster 95th-percentile latency satisfies r^95(t)≤rtarget=80.0 ms\hat{r}_{95}(t) \le r_{\text{target}} = 80.0\text{ ms}r^95​(t)≤rtarget​=80.0 ms.
  2. Both criteria hold continuously for at least three consecutive seconds (tstable=3.0 st_{\text{stable}} = 3.0\text{ s}tstable​=3.0 s).

K. Statistical Inference and Multi-Testing Corrections

Because simulation runs share Common Random Numbers, all statistical analyses are conducted on paired difference distributions:

Δs,B−A=Ms,B−Ms,AandΔs,C−B=Ms,C−Ms,Bfor s∈[1001,1030]\Delta_{s, B-A} = M_{s, B} - M_{s, A} \quad \text{and} \quad \Delta_{s, C-B} = M_{s, C} - M_{s, B} \quad \text{for } s \in [1001, 1030]Δs,B−A​=Ms,B​−Ms,A​andΔs,C−B​=Ms,C​−Ms,B​for s∈[1001,1030]
(27)

Statistical Testing Protocol:

  1. Normality Assessment: The Shapiro-Wilk test (α=0.05\alpha = 0.05α=0.05) is applied to each paired difference vector [12].
  2. Hypothesis Testing:
    • If paired differences are normally distributed: Two-tailed Paired Student's t-test.
    • If paired differences violate normality: Non-parametric Wilcoxon Signed-Rank test [13].
    • Alpha threshold: α=0.05\alpha = 0.05α=0.05.
  3. Effect Size Quantification: Standardized effect sizes are calculated as paired Cohen's dzd_zdz​ [14]:
dz=DˉsDd_z = \frac{\bar{D}}{s_D}dz​=sD​Dˉ​
(28)

Where Dˉ\bar{D}Dˉ is the mean paired difference and sDs_DsD​ is the sample standard deviation of paired differences. For non-parametric comparisons, the rank-biserial correlation rrr is reported. 4. Confidence Intervals: Exact 95% confidence intervals are computed for all paired mean differences: Dˉ±t0.975,29⋅sD30\bar{D} \pm t_{0.975, 29} \cdot \frac{s_D}{\sqrt{30}}Dˉ±t0.975,29​⋅30​sD​​. 5. Multiple Comparison Corrections: Across 120 statistical comparisons conducted in the primary analysis, multi-testing adjustments are enforced across all m=114m = 114m=114 non-trivial hypotheses:

  • Bonferroni Correction (FWER): pBonf=min⁡(1.0,p×114)p_{\text{Bonf}} = \min(1.0, p \times 114)pBonf​=min(1.0,p×114) [15].
  • Benjamini-Hochberg Correction (FDR): False Discovery Rate controlled at q≤0.05q \le 0.05q≤0.05 [16].

Mechanics of Unusually Large Effect Sizes:

Under CRN variance reduction, presenting identical workloads to both configurations creates strong positive covariance between outcomes (Cov(X,Y)≈Var(X)≈Var(Y)\text{Cov}(X, Y) \approx \text{Var}(X) \approx \text{Var}(Y)Cov(X,Y)≈Var(X)≈Var(Y)). Because the variance of paired differences is:

Var(D)=Var(X)+Var(Y)−2Cov(X,Y)\text{Var}(D) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y) - 2\text{Cov}(X, Y)Var(D)=Var(X)+Var(Y)−2Cov(X,Y)
(29)

sDs_DsD​ collapses to near zero (e.g., sD=0.3377%s_D = 0.3377\%sD​=0.3377% in Flash Crowd). Dividing an authentic substantial physical difference (Dˉ=−41.10%\bar{D} = -41.10\%Dˉ=−41.10%) by this minute standard deviation yields massive dzd_zdz​ values (dz=−121.71d_z = -121.71dz​=−121.71). These effect sizes are not calculation artifacts or numerical errors; they reflect the genuine physical impact of a major control intervention evaluated under rigorous variance reduction.

L. Right-Censoring and Horizon-Substitution Limitations

In scenarios involving server crashes, if an experimental run fails to satisfy the DEC-010 restoration criteria prior to the end of the simulation (t=1000.0 st = 1000.0\text{ s}t=1000.0 s), the recovery duration cannot be physically observed. The observation window ends at t=1000.0 st = 1000.0\text{ s}t=1000.0 s, which occurs 550.0 s550.0\text{ s}550.0 s after server repair (t=450.0 st = 450.0\text{ s}t=450.0 s). Such runs are flagged as right-censored at Tcensor=550.0 sT_{\text{censor}} = 550.0\text{ s}Tcensor​=550.0 s with recovered = False.

[!CAUTION] Explicit Methodological Disclosure:

  1. Heuristic Single Imputation: Substituting the observation horizon (550.0 s550.0\text{ s}550.0 s) for unrecovered runs is a standard right-censoring truncation heuristic. It is NOT formal survival analysis (such as the Kaplan-Meier product-limit estimator [17] or semi-parametric Cox proportional hazards modeling).
  2. Speedup Dependence on Horizon Duration: The numerical speedup ratio (e.g., 2.15×2.15\times2.15×) is an empirical finding under the 550.0 s550.0\text{ s}550.0 s horizon, not a mathematically proven lower bound. If the simulation were extended indefinitely, unrecovered runs in both CFG-B and CFG-C (such as seed 1018) would eventually recover at unknown timestamps, shifting the true ratio.
  3. Dual Reporting Requirement: To guarantee complete scientific transparency, all recovery evaluations must report both full-sample imputed statistics (N=30N=30N=30) and uncensored restricted subset statistics (N=25,26,29N=25, 26, 29N=25,26,29), accompanied by explicit censored counts.

VII. RESULTS AND EVALUATION

In this section, we present the empirical results from the frozen CloudRescue experimental corpus. All findings are derived strictly from the pre-registered 360-run primary evaluation battery (3 configurations×4 scenarios×30 matched seeds3\text{ configurations} \times 4\text{ scenarios} \times 30\text{ matched seeds}3 configurations×4 scenarios×30 matched seeds) and the 144-run exploratory sensitivity analysis. In strict accordance with our pre-registered methodology, all comparisons between configurations are conducted on matched seeds utilizing Common Random Numbers (CRN) stream isolation.

B. SLA Compliance and Latency Analysis

The empirical evaluation demonstrates that brownout adaptation provides decisive protection against queue saturation and cascading timeouts across all stress scenarios.

Primary Comparisons Against Unmanaged Baseline (CFG-A):

In the unmanaged baseline (CFG-A), server instances attempt to process all mandatory and optional features regardless of queue depth. Under nominal load (λ=80 req/s\lambda = 80\text{ req/s}λ=80 req/s), queuing delays push the 95th-percentile response latency to 163.15 ms163.15\text{ ms}163.15 ms, causing an overall SLA failure rate of 26.54%26.54\%26.54% despite full availability (Sr=96.08%S_r = 96.08\%Sr​=96.08%). When exposed to severe stress shocks:

  1. Flash Crowd: Unmitigated demand surges saturate FIFO buffers (Qmax⁡=50Q_{\max} = 50Qmax​=50), dropping 34.17%34.17\%34.17% of submitted requests via queue saturation and head-of-line timeouts (SrS_rSr​ collapses to 65.83%65.83\%65.83%). Surviving requests experience inflated latencies (P95=184.34 msP_{95} = 184.34\text{ ms}P95​=184.34 ms), driving the overall SLA failure rate to 44.04%44.04\%44.04%. CloudRescue (CFG-C) reduces overall SLA failures to 2.94%2.94\%2.94%, achieving an absolute 41.1041.1041.10 percentage-point reduction (93.32%\mathbf{93.32\%}93.32% relative reduction, p<10−60p < 10^{-60}p<10−60).
  2. Server Crash: Halving active cluster compute instances drives baseline SLA failure rate to 33.38%33.38\%33.38% (P95=176.57 msP_{95} = 176.57\text{ ms}P95​=176.57 ms). CloudRescue (CFG-C) restricts failures to 6.33%6.33\%6.33%, achieving a 27.0527.0527.05 percentage-point reduction (81.04%\mathbf{81.04\%}81.04% relative reduction, p=5.32×10−53p = 5.32 \times 10^{-53}p=5.32×10−53).
  3. Compound Stress: The confluence of a 3×3\times3× traffic surge and 50%50\%50% capacity loss overwhelms baseline capacity (ρ=4.80\rho = 4.80ρ=4.80), causing catastrophic connection drops (Sr=61.58%S_r = 61.58\%Sr​=61.58%) and driving baseline SLA failures to 47.70%47.70\%47.70%. CloudRescue improves transaction completion to 86.84%86.84\%86.84% and reduces overall SLA failures to 35.33%35.33\%35.33%, representing a 12.3712.3712.37 percentage-point reduction (25.93%\mathbf{25.93\%}25.93% relative reduction, p=6.57×10−46p = 6.57 \times 10^{-46}p=6.57×10−46).

Critical Comparative Analysis Between CFG-B and CFG-C:

A core scientific contribution of this ablation study is the granular examination of where Brownout-Aware Load Balancing (CFG-C) outperforms or underperforms local brownout control alone (CFG-B):

  1. Where CFG-C Outperforms CFG-B (Demand-Side Shocks):
    Under the Flash Crowd scenario, BALB demonstrates clear superiority over conventional JSQ:

    • Overall SLA failures drop from 5.69%5.69\%5.69% in CFG-B to 2.94%2.94\%2.94% in CFG-C (−2.75-2.75−2.75 percentage points, p=3.49×10−30p = 3.49 \times 10^{-30}p=3.49×10−30).
    • 95th-percentile latency improves from 102.91 ms102.91\text{ ms}102.91 ms (which breaches the contractual 100 ms100\text{ ms}100 ms SLA) down to 82.87 ms82.87\text{ ms}82.87 ms (well within SLA compliance, −20.04 ms-20.04\text{ ms}−20.04 ms, p=3.92×10−31p = 3.92 \times 10^{-31}p=3.92×10−31).
    • Mean response latency decreases from 31.47 ms31.47\text{ ms}31.47 ms to 27.05 ms27.05\text{ ms}27.05 ms (−4.41 ms-4.41\text{ ms}−4.41 ms, p=5.57×10−30p = 5.57 \times 10^{-30}p=5.57×10−30).

  2. Where CFG-B Outperforms CFG-C (Capacity-Side Outages):
    Conversely, under Server Crash and Compound Stress, local brownout under JSQ (CFG-B) achieves lower SLA violation rates than BALB (CFG-C):

    • In Server Crash, overall SLA failure in CFG-B is 4.90%4.90\%4.90% compared to 6.33%6.33\%6.33% in CFG-C (+1.43+1.43+1.43 percentage points higher in CFG-C, p=8.62×10−25p = 8.62 \times 10^{-25}p=8.62×10−25).
    • In Compound Stress, overall SLA failure in CFG-B is 33.38%33.38\%33.38% compared to 35.33%35.33\%35.33% in CFG-C (+1.95+1.95+1.95 percentage points higher in CFG-C, p=1.73×10−6p = 1.73 \times 10^{-6}p=1.73×10−6).
    • In Server Crash, 95th-percentile latency in CFG-B remains within SLA at 98.72 ms98.72\text{ ms}98.72 ms, whereas in CFG-C it rises slightly to 104.08 ms104.08\text{ ms}104.08 ms (+5.36 ms+5.36\text{ ms}+5.36 ms).

Architectural Mechanism Behind the Trade-Off:

This performance inversion is not an implementation flaw; it directly reflects the physical mechanics of the Join-Shortest-Queue pathology:

  • In CFG-B, the degraded workers shed optional logic, process requests in 10 ms10\text{ ms}10 ms, and empty their buffers rapidly. JSQ funnels the vast majority of incoming traffic onto these degraded workers. The non-degraded workers retain long queues or low throughput, but the few requests they do complete experience low queuing interference from incoming bursts. This creates an artificial, two-tier cluster state where degraded workers absorb the shock at high speed.
  • In CFG-C, BALB actively penalizes degraded workers (Scorew=αθw−βqwQmax⁡−γUwScore_w = \alpha \theta_w - \beta \frac{q_w}{Q_{\max}} - \gamma U_wScorew​=αθw​−βQmax​qw​​−γUw​), routing requests across all active workers to equalize load. By redirecting requests onto healthy instances, BALB prevents worker starvation and restores equity (J≥0.990J \ge 0.990J≥0.990), but slightly increases queue backlogs across the cluster. Consequently, tail latency on previously sheltered workers increases slightly, producing a modest rise in latency SLA violations (Vlat=5.45%V_{\text{lat}} = 5.45\%Vlat​=5.45% vs 4.82%4.82\%4.82%).

C. Adaptation Recovery Dynamics

We analyze the speed with which the closed-loop feedback controller stabilizes service response latency during an active stress event (TadaptT_{\text{adapt}}Tadapt​).

Adaptation Recovery Time (T_adapt) During Active Stress:
CFG-A (Baseline):      [========================================] 150.0s (Censored: Never Adapts)
CFG-B (Brownout Only): [================] 56.8s
CFG-C (Full BALB):     [=] 2.0s - 2.5s (22.7x to 28.4x Faster, p < 10^-5)

  1. Flash Crowd Scenario:

    • In CFG-A, baseline response latency remains severely elevated throughout the 150-second surge, failing to recover prior to shock termination (Tadapt=150.0 sT_{\text{adapt}} = 150.0\text{ s}Tadapt​=150.0 s, right-censored across 100% of runs).
    • In CFG-B, local PI feedback controllers require 56.73±8.81 s56.73 \pm 8.81\text{ s}56.73±8.81 s to drive dimmers downward and stabilize rolling 95th-percentile latency below 100.0 ms100.0\text{ ms}100.0 ms.
    • In CFG-C, BALB accelerates adaptation to 2.50±2.74 s2.50 \pm 2.74\text{ s}2.50±2.74 s (median 2.00 s2.00\text{ s}2.00 s), achieving a 22.7×22.7\times22.7× speedup over CFG-B (Paired difference Dˉ=−54.23 s\bar{D} = -54.23\text{ s}Dˉ=−54.23 s, p=2.85×10−24p = 2.85 \times 10^{-24}p=2.85×10−24, Cohen's dz=−5.89d_z = -5.89dz​=−5.89). By dynamically coordinating routing scores with dimmer states, BALB immediately distributes load away from congested nodes, allowing local PI controllers to stabilize almost instantaneously.

  2. Server Crash Scenario:

    • In CFG-A, aggregate capacity remains halved, and latency remains above SLA throughout the outage (Tadapt=150.0 sT_{\text{adapt}} = 150.0\text{ s}Tadapt​=150.0 s).
    • In CFG-B, workers adapt in 56.80±32.79 s56.80 \pm 32.79\text{ s}56.80±32.79 s.
    • In CFG-C, adaptation occurs in 2.00±0.00 s2.00 \pm 0.00\text{ s}2.00±0.00 s, representing a 28.4×28.4\times28.4× speedup over CFG-B (p=1.81×10−5p = 1.81 \times 10^{-5}p=1.81×10−5, rank-biserial correlation r=−1.00r = -1.00r=−1.00).

  3. Compound Stress Scenario:

    • Under the combined 3×3\times3× traffic burst and 50%50\%50% server outage (ρ=4.80\rho = 4.80ρ=4.80), aggregate request arrival rate (240 req/s240\text{ req/s}240 req/s) exceeds even the fully degraded cluster capacity (2×100 req/s=200 req/s2 \times 100\text{ req/s} = 200\text{ req/s}2×100 req/s=200 req/s).
    • While all controllers decrement dimmers to θw=0.0\theta_w = 0.0θw​=0.0 within seconds, the structural physical overload forces worker queues to remain saturated throughout the disruption. Consequently, rolling 95th-percentile latency cannot drop below 100.0 ms100.0\text{ ms}100.0 ms while the compound shock persists. Both CFG-B and CFG-C record Tadapt=150.0 sT_{\text{adapt}} = 150.0\text{ s}Tadapt​=150.0 s (right-censored at shock end).

[!IMPORTANT] Methodological Disclosure on Horizon Substitution:
In accordance with our pre-registered methodology, substituting the observation cutoff (550.0 s550.0\text{ s}550.0 s) for unrecovered runs is a single-imputation heuristic. It does not constitute formal non-parametric survival analysis (such as Kaplan-Meier product-limit estimators [17]) or semi-parametric Cox proportional hazards modeling. Furthermore, the empirical speedup ratios (2.15×2.15\times2.15× and 2.06×2.06\times2.06×) represent descriptive findings under the fixed 550-second horizon and must not be interpreted as mathematically proven theoretical lower bounds.

E. Fairness and Service-Fidelity Trade-off

A central finding of this research is the empirical demonstration of a fundamental architectural trade-off between workload distribution equity and optional service fidelity when brownout-aware routing is introduced.

The Fairness vs. Service-Fidelity Trade-Off:
                      Jain's Fairness (J)      Service Fidelity (F)

CFG-C (Full BALB):     [==========  ] 0.98-1.00  [===        ]  9.5%-13.8%
