1. Decisive Support for Load Fairness Improvement (H1,3H_{1,3}H1,3​ — Fairness Dimension):

Under Join-Shortest-Queue (CFG-B), the brownout controller induces extreme load imbalance. Because degraded workers clear their queues rapidly (10 ms10\text{ ms}10 ms mandatory service), JSQ constantly directs arriving requests to the degraded instances, starving healthy workers operating at full fidelity (40 ms40\text{ ms}40 ms). This drives Jain's fairness index down to pathological levels:

  • Nominal: J=0.607±0.003J = 0.607 \pm 0.003J=0.607±0.003
  • Flash Crowd: J=0.730±0.005J = 0.730 \pm 0.005J=0.730±0.005
  • Server Crash: J=0.646±0.004J = 0.646 \pm 0.004J=0.646±0.004
  • Compound Stress: J=0.764±0.010J = 0.764 \pm 0.010J=0.764±0.010

CloudRescue (CFG-C) completely resolves this routing pathology. By incorporating worker dimmer elasticity (αθw\alpha \theta_wαθw​), normalized queue backlog (−βqwQmax⁡-\beta \frac{q_w}{Q_{\max}}−βQmax​qw​​), and CPU utilization (−γUw-\gamma U_w−γUw​), BALB restores near-perfect workload equity across all active workers:

  • Nominal: J=0.981±0.018J = 0.981 \pm 0.018J=0.981±0.018 (ΔJ=+0.374\Delta J = +0.374ΔJ=+0.374, p=1.73×10−6p = 1.73 \times 10^{-6}p=1.73×10−6)
  • Flash Crowd: J=0.989±0.008J = 0.989 \pm 0.008J=0.989±0.008 (ΔJ=+0.259\Delta J = +0.259ΔJ=+0.259, p=1.05×10−42p = 1.05 \times 10^{-42}p=1.05×10−42)
  • Server Crash: J=0.990±0.010J = 0.990 \pm 0.010J=0.990±0.010 (ΔJ=+0.343\Delta J = +0.343ΔJ=+0.343, p=1.86×10−9p = 1.86 \times 10^{-9}p=1.86×10−9)
  • Compound Stress: J=0.996±0.006J = 0.996 \pm 0.006J=0.996±0.006 (ΔJ=+0.232\Delta J = +0.232ΔJ=+0.232, p=1.56×10−38p = 1.56 \times 10^{-38}p=1.56×10−38)

The empirical evidence decisively supports the alternative hypothesis that BALB restores workload distribution fairness (p<10−8p < 10^{-8}p<10−8 across all scenarios).

2. Decisive Rejection of Service-Fidelity Superiority (H1,3H_{1,3}H1,3​ — Fidelity Dimension):

While pre-registered hypothesis H1,3H_{1,3}H1,3​ posited that BALB would also improve service fidelity (FFF) by intelligently steering traffic toward high-dimmer workers, the empirical data decisively disproves this hypothesis:

  • In Nominal: FFF drops from 28.53%28.53\%28.53% in CFG-B to 10.59%10.59\%10.59% in CFG-C (−17.94-17.94−17.94 percentage points, p=1.77×10−41p = 1.77 \times 10^{-41}p=1.77×10−41).
  • In Flash Crowd: FFF drops from 20.89%20.89\%20.89% in CFG-B to 9.49%9.49\%9.49% in CFG-C (−11.40-11.40−11.40 percentage points, p=4.64×10−44p = 4.64 \times 10^{-44}p=4.64×10−44).
  • In Server Crash: FFF drops from 29.67%29.67\%29.67% in CFG-B to 13.77%13.77\%13.77% in CFG-C (−15.91-15.91−15.91 percentage points, p=5.44×10−39p = 5.44 \times 10^{-39}p=5.44×10−39).
  • In Compound Stress: FFF drops from 23.04%23.04\%23.04% in CFG-B to 10.47%10.47\%10.47% in CFG-C (−12.56-12.56−12.56 percentage points, p=3.22×10−41p = 3.22 \times 10^{-41}p=3.22×10−41).

3) Architectural Implications of the Trade-Off:

This trade-off reveals a foundational principle for autonomic cloud computing: load balancing equity and optional feature preservation are fundamentally competing objectives under constrained capacity.

  • In CFG-B, higher service fidelity is an illusion created by severe load skew: healthy workers preserve high dimmers (θ≈1.0\theta \approx 1.0θ≈1.0) only because JSQ starves them of traffic.
  • In CFG-C, BALB forces healthy workers to take their fair share of incoming requests. This prevents queue dropouts and latency violations on congested nodes, but the added computational load immediately forces those healthy workers' local feedback controllers to drop their dimmers to maintain the 80 ms80\text{ ms}80 ms latency setpoint. Consequently, cluster-wide fidelity falls.
  • We explicitly report this negative result without modification: BALB trades optional service richness to buy cluster-wide load equity, queue stability, and recovery speed.

Mechanics of Unusually Large Effect Sizes (dz=−121.71d_z = -121.71dz​=−121.71):

In our statistical battery, several paired effect sizes exceed classical Cohen thresholds by wide margins (e.g., dz=−121.71d_z = -121.71dz​=−121.71 for Flash Crowd VoverallV_{\text{overall}}Voverall​). These large magnitudes stem directly from Common Random Numbers (CRN) variance reduction:

  • In paired designs, Cohen's dz=Dˉ/sDd_z = \bar{D} / s_Ddz​=Dˉ/sD​.
  • Under CRN stream isolation, identical arrival timestamps and service requirements are fed to both systems, inducing an extremely high positive correlation between paired runs (Cov(X,Y)→Var(X)\text{Cov}(X, Y) \to \text{Var}(X)Cov(X,Y)→Var(X)).
  • Consequently, the sample standard deviation of paired differences collapses to near-zero (sD=0.3377%s_D = 0.3377\%sD​=0.3377%).
  • Dividing an authentic physical improvement (Dˉ=−41.1033%\bar{D} = -41.1033\%Dˉ=−41.1033%) by 0.3377%0.3377\%0.3377% yields dz=−41.10330.3377=−121.71d_z = \frac{-41.1033}{0.3377} = \mathbf{-121.71}dz​=0.3377−41.1033​=−121.71.
  • Even when evaluated against pooled marginal standard deviation (spooled=0.2195%s_{\text{pooled}} = 0.2195\%spooled​=0.2195%), the effect size remains massive (dpooled=−187.23d_{\text{pooled}} = \mathbf{-187.23}dpooled​=−187.23).

[!CAUTION] Interpretation Limitation:
These astronomical effect sizes confirm that the observed differences are not stochastic noise, but rather deterministic consequences of the control mechanisms under matched inputs. However, high statistical significance and large effect sizes within a simulation model must not be interpreted as proof of identical real-world magnitude in unmodelled production environments with arbitrary network jitter and non-exponential service distributions.

Robustness of Default Weights: The default configuration (α=1.0,β=1.0,γ=0.5\alpha = 1.0, \beta = 1.0, \gamma = 0.5α=1.0,β=1.0,γ=0.5) demonstrates exceptional stability, achieving Voverall=35.34%V_{\text{overall}} = 35.34\%Voverall​=35.34%, J=0.999J = 0.999J=0.999, and Sr=86.93%S_r = 86.93\%Sr​=86.93%.   2. The Danger of Over-Incentivizing Dimmers (α=2.0,β=0.5,γ=0.0\alpha=2.0, \beta=0.5, \gamma=0.0α=2.0,β=0.5,γ=0.0): When the dimmer weight is doubled (α=2.0\alpha = 2.0α=2.0) while queue suppression is weakened (β=0.5\beta = 0.5β=0.5) and CPU utilization is unpenalized (γ=0.0\gamma = 0.0γ=0.0), BALB creates a feedback pathology: it aggressively steers traffic to slightly higher-dimmer nodes before their buffers have cleared. This causes queues to saturate, driving overall SLA failure to its worst observed value (37.21%37.21\%37.21%) and degrading fairness (J=0.825J = 0.825J=0.825).
  3. The Stabilizing Role of CPU Utilization (γ>0\gamma > 0γ>0): Introducing the historical CPU penalty (γ=0.5 or 1.0\gamma = 0.5\text{ or } 1.0γ=0.5 or 1.0) prevents the load balancer from overwhelming workers that recently cleared their queues but are computationally saturated. Across all α\alphaα and β\betaβ settings, activating γ≥0.5\gamma \ge 0.5γ≥0.5 consistently elevates Jain's fairness index (J≥0.971J \ge 0.971J≥0.971, with J≥0.985J \ge 0.985J≥0.985 for all β≤1.5\beta \le 1.5β≤1.5).

In accordance with scientific integrity guidelines, three seeds per cell (n=3n=3n=3) are insufficient to establish a global mathematical optimum; this sweep confirms the robustness of the parameter region rather than proving a single optimal coordinate.

VIII. DISCUSSION AND LIMITATIONS

The empirical evaluation of CloudRescue establishes that autonomic brownout adaptation and brownout-aware request dispatching fundamentally transform cloud service resilience under severe operational disruptions. In this section, we interpret our primary findings, analyze the underlying feedback and queuing mechanisms, evaluate the architectural trade-offs, discuss practical deployment implications within modern cloud infrastructures, and candidly document the scientific limitations and threats to validity of this study.

A. Interpretation of Main Findings and Physical Resilience Mechanisms

Modern cloud microservices are engineered under the assumption of stationary, well-provisioned operating regimes where queue lengths remain short and response times adhere to contractual percentiles (P95≤100 msP_{95} \le 100\text{ ms}P95​≤100 ms). However, when systems encounter traffic flash crowds (λ=240 req/s\lambda = 240\text{ req/s}λ=240 req/s) or hardware instance crashes (50%50\%50% capacity reduction), the traffic intensity ρ=λμtotal\rho = \frac{\lambda}{\mu_{\text{total}}}ρ=μtotal​λ​ escalates from nominal ρ=0.80\rho = 0.80ρ=0.80 to super-critical regimes (ρ=1.60–4.80\rho = 1.60\text{--}4.80ρ=1.60–4.80). In conventional queueing systems, as ρ→1.0\rho \to 1.0ρ→1.0, mean queue waiting time scales asymptotically as Wq∝ρμ(1−ρ)W_q \propto \frac{\rho}{\mu (1 - \rho)}Wq​∝μ(1−ρ)ρ​. When arrival rates exceed aggregate service capacity (ρ>1.0\rho > 1.0ρ>1.0), request backlogs grow linearly without bound until the physical buffer capacity (Qmax⁡=50Q_{\max} = 50Qmax​=50) is exhausted. Under these unmitigated conditions, as demonstrated by baseline CFG-A, incoming requests suffer catastrophic queue dropouts (Ndrop_queueN_{\text{drop\_queue}}Ndrop_queue​) and connection timeouts (Ndrop_timeoutN_{\text{drop\_timeout}}Ndrop_timeout​ when Wk>200 msW_k > 200\text{ ms}Wk​>200 ms), driving overall SLA failure rates to 44.04%44.04\%44.04% under flash crowd stress and 47.70%47.70\%47.70% under compound stress.

Autonomic brownout adaptation decisively halts this queuing collapse by providing instantaneous, software-level capacity modulation. Rather than waiting for virtual machines or container pods to boot—a provisioning delay that typically spans dozens of seconds to several minutes [1, 5]—brownout alters the application execution profile at microsecond resolution. When the velocity-form discrete PI controller decrements the worker dimmer (θw→0\theta_w \to 0θw​→0), incoming requests bypass the optional enhancement stage (Sopt∼30 msS_{\text{opt}} \sim 30\text{ ms}Sopt​∼30 ms) and execute only mandatory business logic (Smand∼10 msS_{\text{mand}} \sim 10\text{ ms}Smand​∼10 ms). This collapses expected per-request service time from 40 ms40\text{ ms}40 ms down to 10 ms10\text{ ms}10 ms, expanding individual worker throughput capacity from μw=25 req/s\mu_w = 25\text{ req/s}μw​=25 req/s to μw=100 req/s\mu_w = 100\text{ req/s}μw​=100 req/s (400 req/s400\text{ req/s}400 req/s across four workers). This instantaneous 4×4\times4× throughput expansion rapidly deflates queue buffers, ensuring that waiting times remain negligible and driving rolling P95P_{95}P95​ latency below the contractual 100 ms100\text{ ms}100 ms threshold. Consequently, brownout achieves an absolute 41.1041.1041.10 percentage-point reduction in SLA failures (p<10−60p < 10^{-60}p<10−60) during traffic surges, converting catastrophic system outages into gracefully degraded, highly available service delivery.

B. The Join-Shortest-Queue (JSQ) Pathology and BALB's Incremental Contribution

While local brownout controllers effectively regulate individual compute instances, our three-way ablation demonstrates that deploying brownout across a multi-server cluster introduces an acute architectural conflict when paired with conventional load balancing policies like Join-Shortest-Queue (JSQ). In CFG-B, this manifests as the JSQ routing pathology:

  1. When worker www experiences a transient latency increase, its local PI feedback controller decrements its dimmer (θw→0\theta_w \to 0θw​→0) to shed optional logic.
  2. Because worker www now processes requests in only 10 ms10\text{ ms}10 ms (compared to 40 ms40\text{ ms}40 ms for non-degraded peers), its FIFO queue drains four times faster.
  3. JSQ inspects only instantaneous buffer depths (qwq_wqw​) and perceives the degraded worker as possessing the greatest spare capacity.
  4. JSQ immediately funnels an overwhelming proportion of incoming requests to the degraded worker.
  5. Meanwhile, healthy workers operating at full fidelity (θ≈1.0\theta \approx 1.0θ≈1.0) process requests more slowly, retain longer queues, and are starved of incoming requests by JSQ.

This pathology locks the degraded worker into perpetual task shedding, produces severe cluster load skew (J≈0.607–0.764J \approx 0.607\text{--}0.764J≈0.607–0.764), and delays system recovery when disruptions subside. Furthermore, because standard JSQ implementations utilize deterministic tie-breaking (e.g., selecting the lowest worker index on queue depth ties), initial asymmetries become deeply entrenched.

CloudRescue’s Brownout-Aware Load Balancing (BALB) algorithm resolves this pathology by decoupling request dispatching from raw queue depth alone. By evaluating a composite multi-attribute score:

Scorew(t)=α⋅θw(t)−β⋅(qw(t)Qmax⁡)−γ⋅Uw(t)Score_w(t) = \alpha \cdot \theta_w(t) - \beta \cdot \left(\frac{q_w(t)}{Q_{\max}}\right) - \gamma \cdot U_w(t)Scorew​(t)=α⋅θw​(t)−β⋅(Qmax​qw​(t)​)−γ⋅Uw​(t)
(30)

BALB establishes a self-correcting feedback mechanism across the cluster:

  • Dimmer Incentive (αθw\alpha \theta_wαθw​): Arriving requests are guided toward workers operating at higher fidelity, preventing healthy workers from being starved of traffic.
  • Dynamic Queue Suppression (−βqwQmax⁡-\beta \frac{q_w}{Q_{\max}}−βQmax​qw​​): As requests accumulate in a high-fidelity worker's buffer, the normalized queue penalty rapidly counterbalances the dimmer incentive, redirecting traffic before buffer saturation can occur.
  • Historical Utilization Damping (−γUw-\gamma U_w−γUw​): Penalizing cumulative processor utilization prevents the load balancer from overwhelming workers that have temporarily cleared their queues but remain computationally saturated.
  • Soft-Overload Fallback: When aggregate cluster buffers exceed 80%80\%80% occupancy (qw≥Qsoftq_w \ge Q_{\text{soft}}qw​≥Qsoft​), BALB autonomously zeros the dimmer incentive (α=0\alpha = 0α=0), collapsing the policy into pure congestion draining.

Through this formulation, BALB restores near-perfect workload equity across all operational instances (J≥0.981–0.996J \ge 0.981\text{--}0.996J≥0.981–0.996, p<10−8p < 10^{-8}p<10−8) and accelerates adaptation by up to 28.4×28.4\times28.4× (p<2.9×10−24p < 2.9 \times 10^{-24}p<2.9×10−24) during traffic surges.

C. The Fundamental Fairness versus Service-Fidelity Trade-off

A foundational scientific insight of this research is the empirical demonstration of a fundamental architectural trade-off between workload distribution equity and optional service fidelity under constrained capacity:

The Core Architectural Trade-Off:
┌─────────────────────────────────┐               ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│       CFG-B (Brownout Only)     │               │        CFG-C (Full BALB)        │
├─────────────────────────────────┤               ├─────────────────────────────────┤
│ • Jain's Fairness: 0.61 - 0.76  │   ────────►   │ • Jain's Fairness: 0.98 - 1.00  │
│ • Service Fidelity: 20.9% - 29.7%│   (Equitable  │ • Service Fidelity: 9.5% - 13.8% │
│ • Pathological queue skew       │    Routing)   │ • Broad cluster-wide degradation│
│ • Artificial fidelity shelter   │               │ • High tail-latency predictability│
└─────────────────────────────────┘               └─────────────────────────────────┘

While pre-registered hypothesis H1,3H_{1,3}H1,3​ anticipated that BALB would simultaneously improve workload fairness (JJJ) and service fidelity (FFF) by steering traffic toward high-dimmer workers, the empirical evaluation decisively rejected the fidelity hypothesis (p<10−38p < 10^{-38}p<10−38). Across all four operational scenarios, CFG-C exhibited significantly lower service fidelity than CFG-B:

  • In Nominal: FFF dropped from 28.53%28.53\%28.53% to 10.59%10.59\%10.59% (−17.94 pp-17.94\text{ pp}−17.94 pp, p=1.77×10−41p = 1.77 \times 10^{-41}p=1.77×10−41).
  • In Flash Crowd: FFF dropped from 20.89%20.89\%20.89% to 9.49%9.49\%9.49% (−11.40 pp-11.40\text{ pp}−11.40 pp, p=4.64×10−44p = 4.64 \times 10^{-44}p=4.64×10−44).
  • In Server Crash: FFF dropped from 29.67%29.67\%29.67% to 13.77%13.77\%13.77% (−15.91 pp-15.91\text{ pp}−15.91 pp, p=5.44×10−39p = 5.44 \times 10^{-39}p=5.44×10−39).
  • In Compound Stress: FFF dropped from 23.04%23.04\%23.04% to 10.47%10.47\%10.47% (−12.56 pp-12.56\text{ pp}−12.56 pp, p=3.22×10−41p = 3.22 \times 10^{-41}p=3.22×10−41).

Architectural Mechanism:

This trade-off is not an engineering defect; it is a physical consequence of closed-loop feedback coupling. In CFG-B, high cluster service fidelity (F≈21%–30%F \approx 21\%\text{--}30\%F≈21%–30%) is an illusion sustained by severe load skew: healthy workers preserve high dimmers (θ≈1.0\theta \approx 1.0θ≈1.0) only because JSQ starves them of incoming requests while dumping traffic onto degraded nodes. In CFG-C, BALB eliminates this routing bias by forcing healthy workers to take their equitable share of incoming requests. However, as healthy workers receive additional traffic, their queue depths increase, pushing their 95th-percentile response latency toward the setpoint (rtarget=80 msr_{\text{target}} = 80\text{ ms}rtarget​=80 ms). To maintain latency compliance, those workers' local PI feedback controllers are forced to drop their dimmers, causing a wider fraction of the cluster to operate in degraded mode.

Consequently, BALB intentionally sacrifices optional feature richness to purchase cluster-wide load equity, buffer stability, and tail latency predictability. Service operators deploying brownout-aware routing must explicitly recognize this trade-off: under severe resource constraints, equitable workload distribution inherently depresses aggregate feature richness.

D. Adaptation and Post-Restoration Recovery Dynamics

Our evaluation decoupled recovery into two distinct operational phases: adaptation during active stress (TadaptT_{\text{adapt}}Tadapt​) and post-restoration recovery following server repair (TrestoreT_{\text{restore}}Trestore​).

  1. Adaptation Dynamics During Stress:
    During active traffic surges, unmanaged baseline systems (CFG-A) completely fail to adapt (Tadapt=150.0 sT_{\text{adapt}} = 150.0\text{ s}Tadapt​=150.0 s, right-censored). Brownout alone (CFG-B) requires 56.73–56.80 s56.73\text{--}56.80\text{ s}56.73–56.80 s for local controllers to pull dimmers downward against incoming queue backlogs. BALB (CFG-C) accelerates this stabilization to 2.00–2.50 s2.00\text{--}2.50\text{ s}2.00–2.50 s, achieving a 22.7×22.7\times22.7× to 28.4×28.4\times28.4× speedup (p<2.9×10−24p < 2.9 \times 10^{-24}p<2.9×10−24). By coordinating routing scores with dimmer states, BALB steers traffic away from overwhelmed instances the instant latency spikes, providing the local controllers with immediate breathing room to achieve stable equilibrium. Under Compound Stress, however, physical demand (240 req/s240\text{ req/s}240 req/s) strictly exceeds even fully degraded cluster capacity (200 req/s200\text{ req/s}200 req/s), preventing any controller from stabilizing response times below SLA while the combined disruption persists (Tadapt=150.0 sT_{\text{adapt}} = 150.0\text{ s}Tadapt​=150.0 s across all configurations).

  2. Nominal-Referenced Post-Restoration Recovery (DEC-010):
    A critical methodological contribution of this research is establishing DEC-010 for post-repair recovery. In prior literature, recovery has frequently been judged against arbitrary static dimmer thresholds (e.g., θˉ≥0.95\bar{\theta} \ge 0.95θˉ≥0.95). However, our discrete-event simulations demonstrate that under nominal stationary load (λ=80 req/s\lambda = 80\text{ req/s}λ=80 req/s) and tight latency setpoints (rtarget=80 msr_{\text{target}} = 80\text{ ms}rtarget​=80 ms), stable closed-loop feedback controllers naturally settle at equilibrium dimmers well below unity (θnom∗∈[0.05,0.55]\theta_{\text{nom}}^* \in [0.05, 0.55]θnom∗​∈[0.05,0.55]). Demanding that restored instances achieve an unachievable static threshold near 1.01.01.0 results in severe artificial right-censoring.

    By evaluating recovery against empirical, seed- and worker-specific nominal steady-state baselines (θw≥0.95⋅θnom∗(c,s,w)\theta_w \ge 0.95 \cdot \theta_{\text{nom}}^*(c, s, w)θw​≥0.95⋅θnom∗​(c,s,w)), DEC-010 provides an objective, un-censored recovery metric. Under DEC-010, BALB accelerates post-restoration recovery by 2.06×2.06\times2.06× to 2.15×2.15\times2.15× (p<4.1×10−5p < 4.1 \times 10^{-5}p<4.1×10−5 across paired tests), increasing 30-seed full restoration rates from 83.3%–86.7%83.3\%\text{--}86.7\%83.3%–86.7% in CFG-B to 96.7%96.7\%96.7% in CFG-C. BALB achieves this superior recovery because it routes traffic equitably to restored instances as their dimmers ramp up, whereas JSQ floods repaired workers the instant their queues empty, repeatedly re-triggering local dimmer drops.

E. Sensitivity Analysis & Parameter Robustness

The exploratory 144-run parameter sweep across 48 weight combinations in BALB’s scoring function (Scorew=αθw−βqwQmax⁡−γUwScore_w = \alpha \theta_w - \beta \frac{q_w}{Q_{\max}} - \gamma U_wScorew​=αθw​−βQmax​qw​​−γUw​) provides crucial guidance for autonomic system tuning:

  1. Broad Stability of Default Weights:
    Across all 24 configurations where β≥1.0\beta \ge 1.0β≥1.0 and γ≥0.5\gamma \ge 0.5γ≥0.5, overall SLA failures vary within an extremely narrow band (34.70%34.70\%34.70% to 35.67%35.67\%35.67%). This confirms that BALB is highly robust against minor parameter misconfigurations and does not exhibit brittle edge-of-stability dynamics.
  2. The Peril of Dimmer Over-Incentivization:
    When the dimmer weight is heavily prioritized while queue suppression is weakened and CPU utilization is unpenalized (α=2.0,β=0.5,γ=0.0\alpha = 2.0, \beta = 0.5, \gamma = 0.0α=2.0,β=0.5,γ=0.0), BALB exhibits pathological behavior: it aggressively steers traffic to slightly higher-dimmer nodes before their buffers have cleared. This rapidly saturates queues, driving SLA failure to its worst observed rate (37.21%37.21\%37.21%) and degrading fairness (J=0.825J = 0.825J=0.825).
  3. The Stabilizing Role of CPU Utilization:
    Activating the historical CPU utilization penalty (γ≥0.5\gamma \ge 0.5γ≥0.5) consistently elevates Jain's fairness index (J≥0.971J \ge 0.971J≥0.971, with J≥0.985J \ge 0.985J≥0.985 for all β≤1.5\beta \le 1.5β≤1.5). By penalizing cumulative processor busy time, BALB prevents the proxy from dispatching bursts of requests to workers that have momentarily emptied their queues but remain computationally saturated.

F. Practical Implications for Autonomic Cloud Management

Grounded in the cloud resilience taxonomy of Welsh and Benkhelifa [1] and the Resilinets architecture of Sterbenz et al. [4], CloudRescue operates primarily across the Remediate and Recover phases of the D2R2+DRD^2R^2 + DRD2R2+DR operational cycle:

  • Remediate: Instantaneous task shedding bounded by soft-overload fallbacks mitigates acute queue saturation during flash crowds and server dropouts.
  • Recover: Brownout-aware load balancing coordinates workload re-admission, accelerating cluster return to healthy operational equilibria without re-inducing secondary queuing collapses.

In practical cloud-native production environments (such as Kubernetes clusters fronted by Envoy or Istio service meshes), CloudRescue offers significant operational advantages:

  • Bridging the Provisioning Delay Gap: Horizontal Pod Autoscalers (HPA) and cloud VM provisioning require between 30 seconds30\text{ seconds}30 seconds and several minutes to detect sustained overload, schedule pods, pull container images, and initialize runtime environments [1, 5]. CloudRescue provides instantaneous, sub-second protection during this transient provisioning window, shedding optional tasks until reactive auto-scalers can instantiate additional physical instances.
  • Service Mesh Implementation: BALB can be directly implemented as an Envoy HTTP filter using WebAssembly (WASM), evaluating lightweight dimmer headers returned in upstream response metadata without requiring out-of-band coordination.
  • Decomposition Guidelines: Microservice developers should partition service contracts into mandatory transactional paths (e.g., checkout, order persistence) and optional enhancement paths (e.g., personalized recommendations, speculative pre-computations), exposing dimmer probabilities via local middleware decorators.

G. Threats to Validity and Scientific Limitations

To maintain the highest standards of scientific integrity, we explicitly document the limitations and threats to validity inherent in this study:

  1. Simulation-Based Scope vs. Production Cloud Environments (External Validity):
    This evaluation was conducted entirely within a discrete-event simulation model (SimPy [9]) with microsecond event scheduling. While discrete-event simulation provides complete determinism, perfect reproducible stream isolation, and eliminates uncontrolled background noise (such as OS scheduling interrupts, hypervisor CPU overcommitment, and garbage collection pauses), it does not capture complex physical-layer phenomena such as TCP connection window dynamics, network switch buffer bloat, hardware memory bus contention, or asynchronous distributed clock drift. Consequently, while relative algorithmic trade-offs are rigorously established, absolute latency values must be validated in production testbeds prior to enterprise deployment.
  2. Workload and Execution Time Distributions (Construct Validity):
    Request inter-arrival intervals and component execution durations were modeled using standard Markovian exponential distributions. In production cloud microservices, execution times frequently follow heavy-tailed distributions (such as Pareto or log-normal distributions) where occasional large requests can cause head-of-line blocking. The impact of heavy-tailed service times on PI controller stability and BALB queue penalties represents an important open research question.
  3. Cumulative Utilization Inertia (Internal Validity):
    In BALB, worker utilization is defined as cumulative processor busy time divided by operational uptime (Tbusy,w/Toperational,wT_{\text{busy}, w} / T_{\text{operational}, w}Tbusy,w​/Toperational,w​). While cumulative utilization provides exceptional long-term stability, it responds sluggishly to sudden, short-duration workload changes after extended periods of nominal operation. In production environments, an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) or sliding-window utilization metric may provide faster responsiveness to abrupt traffic shifts.
  4. Deterministic Join-Shortest-Queue Baseline (Internal Validity):
    The baseline JSQ routing policy evaluated in CFG-A and CFG-B employs deterministic tie-breaking (selecting the lowest worker index on queue depth ties). While this reflects standard FIFO proxy implementations, an auxiliary comparative baseline evaluating randomized tie-breaking (Randomized JSQ / JSQ-R) was not implemented in this experimental battery.
  5. Exploratory Sensitivity Sample Size (Statistical Conclusion Validity):
    The multi-factor parameter sweep across BALB routing weights evaluated 48 combinations over n=3n = 3n=3 seeds per cell (144 runs144\text{ runs}144 runs). While this sweep confirms the broad stability and boundaries of the parameter landscape, three seeds per cell provide insufficient statistical power to identify a single globally optimal mathematical coordinate. Top-ranking parameter configurations are reported strictly as exploratory observations.
  6. Right-Censoring Horizon Substitution (Statistical Conclusion Validity):
    In our post-restoration recovery evaluation, substituting the 550.0-second observation cutoff for unrecovered runs represents a heuristic single-imputation approach. It does not constitute formal non-parametric survival analysis (such as the Kaplan-Meier product-limit estimator [17] or semi-parametric Cox proportional hazards modeling). The observed speedup ratios (2.06×2.06\times2.06× to 2.15×2.15\times2.15×) are descriptive findings under the fixed horizon and should not be interpreted as mathematically proven theoretical lower bounds.
  7. Lower Service Fidelity in BALB (Construct Validity):
    As candidly reported, full BALB (CFG-C) consistently delivers lower service fidelity (F=9.5%–13.8%F = 9.5\%\text{--}13.8\%F=9.5%–13.8%) than uncoordinated brownout (CFG-B, F=20.9%–29.7%F = 20.9\%\text{--}29.7\%F=20.9%–29.7%). Service providers whose business models heavily prioritize optional feature execution over workload distribution equity may find BALB’s aggressive degradation counter-productive unless weighting parameters (α,β,γ\alpha, \beta, \gammaα,β,γ) are tuned specifically to favor fidelity.
  8. Single-Tier Cluster Scope (External Validity):
    Our modeled architecture comprises a single centralized ingress proxy fronting a single-tier worker cluster (M=4M=4M=4). Modern enterprise cloud applications typically consist of deep, multi-tier microservice call graphs with cascading dependencies. Recursive brownout propagation across multi-tier topologies remains an open avenue for future investigation.

IX. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK

A. Summary of Contributions

In this paper, we presented CloudRescue, an autonomic cloud resilience framework that unites local closed-loop brownout feedback control with brownout-aware multi-attribute request dispatching to protect cloud microservices from catastrophic queuing degradation during severe operational shocks. Modern cloud systems face acute vulnerability to traffic flash crowds and hardware dropouts; traditional mitigation via hardware over-provisioning is economically prohibitive, while reactive auto-scaling suffers from non-negligible provisioning delays that leave systems unprotected during the onset of disruptions [1, 5].

To address these limitations, CloudRescue introduced three core architectural and methodological contributions:

  1. Velocity-Form Discrete PI Brownout Controller with Intrinsic Anti-Windup: We formulated an autonomous, per-worker feedback controller that modulates the execution probability of optional software features (θw∈[0,1]\theta_w \in [0, 1]θw​∈[0,1]). By computing control candidates directly from clamped outputs, incorporating an insufficient-sample hold mechanism, and suppressing derivative kicks during telemetry resumption, our controller provides stable, sub-second capacity modulation without integral windup lag.
  2. Brownout-Aware Load Balancing (BALB): We formulated a multi-attribute dispatch scoring algorithm (Scorew=αθw−βqwQmax⁡−γUwScore_w = \alpha \theta_w - \beta \frac{q_w}{Q_{\max}} - \gamma U_wScorew​=αθw​−βQmax​qw​​−γUw​) that decouples dispatching from raw queue depth, incorporates dynamic queue back-off penalties, and enforces an autonomic soft-overload fallback. BALB resolves the pathological load skew of Join-Shortest-Queue under brownout, restoring near-perfect load balance across active workers (J≥0.981–0.996J \ge 0.981\text{--}0.996J≥0.981–0.996).
  3. Rigorous Three-Way Ablation and Reproducible Discrete-Event Framework: Evaluated across 360 primary simulation runs with 5-stream PRNG Common Random Numbers stream isolation and a 144-run exploratory sensitivity sweep, our study cleanly isolated baseline operation (CFG-A), local brownout alone (CFG-B), and full BALB (CFG-C). We introduced the DEC-010 nominal-referenced recovery methodology to eliminate artificial right-censoring in post-repair evaluation, establishing that BALB accelerates post-restoration recovery by 2.06×2.06\times2.06× to 2.15×2.15\times2.15× (p<4.1×10−5p < 4.1 \times 10^{-5}p<4.1×10−5). Crucially, our empirical analysis characterized the fundamental trade-off between workload distribution equity and optional service fidelity, showing that BALB intentionally sacrifices feature richness (FFF) by 11.411.411.4 to 15.915.915.9 percentage points (p<10−38p < 10^{-38}p<10−38) to maintain cluster-wide queue stability and SLA compliance.

B. Future Research Directions

The findings and limitations documented in this research highlight several promising avenues for future investigation:

  1. Multi-Tier Microservice Dependency Topologies: While CloudRescue modeled an ingress proxy fronting a single-tier worker pool, modern enterprise applications consist of complex directed acyclic graph (DAG) call trees. Extending brownout control across multi-tier service graphs requires investigating recursive dimmer propagation, distributed backpressure coordination, and multi-tier BALB dispatching.
  2. Trace-Driven and Heavy-Tailed Workload Evaluation: Future work will evaluate CloudRescue under production cloud traces (e.g., Azure Functions or Alibaba cluster traces) characterized by heavy-tailed service times (Pareto, log-normal) and diurnal arrival patterns, assessing controller convergence and queue penalty dynamics under non-exponential execution profiles.
  3. Online Adaptive Tuning via Machine Learning: While our 144-run sensitivity sweep confirmed the broad stability of default weights (α=1.0,β=1.0,γ=0.5\alpha=1.0, \beta=1.0, \gamma=0.5α=1.0,β=1.0,γ=0.5), online reinforcement learning or Bayesian optimization could dynamically tune routing weights in response to changing traffic burstiness and failure severities.
  4. Physical Cloud Testbed and Service Mesh Deployment: A natural extension is implementing CloudRescue within production-grade service mesh architectures (e.g., Envoy proxy sidecars using WebAssembly filters) deployed on Kubernetes, evaluating real-world interactions with Linux kernel networking, container runtime overheads, and horizontal pod autoscalers.
